items.explanation: Each selected element is treated independently rather than as one region.

items.title: Extrude to Cursor
items.fact: Extrude to Cursor extrudes selected mesh components toward the mouse cursor.
items.explanation: It lets the cursor location define the direction and endpoint of an extrusion.

items.title: Inset Faces
items.fact: Inset Faces creates a smaller face region inside selected faces.
items.explanation: Inset geometry is useful for creating borders and supporting loops.

items.title: Bevel Tool
items.fact: The Bevel tool creates a bevel from selected elements.
items.explanation: Beveling rounds or chamfers hard edges by adding geometry.

items.title: Loop Cut
items.fact: Loop Cut creates an edge loop across a mesh.
items.explanation: Loop cuts add additional edge control for shaping a model.

items.title: Offset Edge Loop Cut
items.fact: Offset Edge Loop Cut adds two edge loops around a selected loop.
items.explanation: The paired loops can provide support around an existing edge region.

items.title: Knife Tool
items.fact: Knife creates a manual cut through mesh geometry.
items.explanation: The user draws the cut path directly in the viewport.

items.title: Knife Confirmation
items.fact: Pressing Enter confirms a Knife cut.
items.explanation: The cut path becomes part of the mesh after confirmation.

items.title: Bisect Tool
items.fact: Bisect cuts a mesh through a plane.
items.explanation: It is useful when a model needs to be sliced along a controlled plane.

items.title: Poly Build
items.fact: Poly Build adds geometry by creating vertices one by one.
items.explanation: It supports manual topology construction.

items.title: Spin Tool
items.fact: Spin creates geometry by extruding and rotating.
items.explanation: This is useful for radial modeling patterns.

items.title: Smooth Tool
items.fact: The Smooth tool flattens angles of selected vertices.
items.explanation: It can soften irregular vertex positions.

items.title: Randomize Tool
items.fact: Randomize perturbs selected vertices.
items.explanation: Controlled randomization can introduce variation into geometry.

items.title: Edge Slide
items.fact: Edge Slide moves an edge loop along a face.
items.explanation: It adjusts topology placement without moving the loop off its supporting surface.

items.title: Vertex Slide
items.fact: Vertex Slide moves a vertex along an edge.
items.explanation: It gives fine control over a vertex’s position along existing topology.

items.title: Shrink Fatten
items.fact: Shrink/Fatten moves selected vertices along their normals.
items.explanation: The operation pushes selected surface regions inward or outward relative to their normals.

items.title: Push Pull
items.fact: Push/Pull moves selected elements away from or toward the pivot point.
items.explanation: It changes the position of selected mesh parts relative to the transform pivot.

items.title: Shear
items.fact: Shear skews selected elements.
items.explanation: The shape is slanted rather than simply translated or scaled.

items.title: To Sphere
items.fact: To Sphere moves vertices toward a spherical shape around the object center.
items.explanation: It is useful for regularizing selected geometry into a spherical form.

items.title: Rip Region
items.fact: Rip Region tears selected polygons and moves the result.
items.explanation: It separates connected mesh regions along the rip operation.

items.title: Rip Edge
items.fact: Rip Edge extends vertices and moves the result.
items.explanation: It can open or separate an edge region.

items.title: Vertex Editing Mode
items.fact: Vertex selection mode is one of Blender’s mesh editing modes.
items.explanation: Selecting vertices gives direct control over mesh points.

items.title: Edge Editing Mode
items.fact: Edge selection mode is one of Blender’s mesh editing modes.
items.explanation: Selecting edges supports operations that act on edge topology.

items.title: Face Editing Mode
items.fact: Face selection mode is one of Blender’s mesh editing modes.
items.explanation: Selecting faces makes surface regions the focus of editing operations.

items.title: Inset Before Extrude
items.fact: Inset Faces can create an inner boundary before a subsequent extrusion.
items.explanation: This makes it possible to create bordered regions within a surface.

items.title: Loop Cuts for Local Control
items.fact: Loop Cut adds topology that can provide additional control over local shape.
items.explanation: Extra edge loops create more locations at which the mesh can be adjusted.

items.title: Bevel for Edge Shape
items.fact: A bevel creates geometry around a selected edge or region.
items.explanation: The added geometry can soften a previously sharp transition.

items.title: Knife for Custom Topology
items.fact: Knife supports manual, user-drawn mesh cuts.
items.explanation: It is appropriate when a predefined loop cut does not follow the desired path.

items.title: Bisect for Planar Cuts
items.fact: Bisect cuts geometry with a plane.
items.explanation: Plane-based cutting is useful when a precise slice is required.

items.title: To Sphere for Regularization
items.fact: To Sphere can turn selected vertex arrangements toward a spherical form.
items.explanation: This is useful for cleaning up approximate circular or spherical selections.

items.title: Edge Slide for Topology Placement
items.fact: Edge Slide changes where an edge lies along its supporting faces.
items.explanation: It can reposition support loops without completely rebuilding surrounding topology.

items.title: Vertex Slide for Fine Placement
items.fact: Vertex Slide moves a vertex along an existing edge.
items.explanation: It offers fine topology adjustment while preserving the edge relationship.

items.title: Shrink Fatten for Surface Offset
items.fact: Shrink/Fatten moves vertices along normals.
items.explanation: It can expand or contract a selected surface region.

items.title: UV Mapping
items.fact: UV mapping is the process of projecting a 2D image texture onto a 3D model's surface.
items.explanation: Think of it like cutting up a cardboard box to lay it perfectly flat on the ground. UV mapping defines exactly how a flat image (like a picture of brick or skin) wraps around the complex geometry of a 3D object.

items.title: UV Coordinates
items.fact: UV coordinates project a 3D model surface onto 2D image space.
items.explanation: The U and V axes are used instead of X, Y, and Z for texture coordinates.

items.title: UV Vertex Correspondence
items.fact: Each point in a UV map corresponds to a mesh vertex.
items.explanation: UV editing changes where the model surface appears in the 2D texture space.

items.title: UV Edge Correspondence
items.fact: Lines joining UV coordinates correspond to mesh edges.
items.explanation: The UV layout mirrors the model topology in a flattened representation.

items.title: UV Face Correspondence
items.fact: Each UV face corresponds to a mesh face.
items.explanation: Flattening preserves the relationship between 3D polygons and their texture regions.

items.title: Multiple UV Textures
items.fact: A face can participate in multiple UV textures.
items.explanation: A mesh can therefore use different UV texture assignments for different images or workflows.

items.title: Default UV State
items.fact: Meshes are not created with UVs by default in the documented workflow.
items.explanation: The artist must create or assign the mapping needed for texture use.

items.title: Edit Mode UV Unwrap
items.fact: UV unwrapping is performed in Edit Mode in the 3D Viewport.
items.explanation: Mesh selection in Edit Mode determines what gets unwrapped.

items.title: Mark Seams
items.fact: Marking seams is part of the general documented UV workflow when seams are needed.
items.explanation: Seams tell the unwrap process where the surface can be cut.

items.title: Unwrap Workflow
items.fact: The documented UV workflow includes selecting mesh faces and choosing an unwrap method.
items.explanation: Unwrapping produces UV islands that can then be edited.

items.title: UV Islands
items.fact: Unwrapping creates one or more UV islands in the UV Editor.
items.explanation: An island is a connected region of UV coordinates separated from others.

items.title: Test Image
items.fact: Blender recommends using a test image to check texture distortion after unwrapping.
items.explanation: A test pattern makes stretching and compression visible.

items.title: Edit UVs
items.fact: After unwrapping, UV coordinates can be adjusted in the UV Editor.
items.explanation: Manual editing can improve layout quality after automatic unwrapping.

items.title: UV Unwrap Node
items.fact: The Geometry Nodes UV Unwrap node generates UV map islands using seam edges.
items.explanation: It provides an unwrapping operation inside node-based geometry workflows.

items.title: UV Unwrap Margin
items.fact: The UV Unwrap node has a Margin input for distance between UV islands.
items.explanation: A margin reduces direct contact between islands in the generated layout.

items.title: UV Unwrap Angle Based
items.fact: The UV Unwrap node supports an Angle Based method.
items.explanation: This method aims to produce a good 2D representation of the mesh.

items.title: UV Unwrap Conformal
items.fact: The UV Unwrap node supports a Conformal method using LSCM.
items.explanation: Blender notes that it is generally less accurate than Angle Based but works better for simpler objects.

items.title: UV Node Pack Islands
items.fact: The UV Unwrap node implicitly performs a Pack Islands operation after unwrapping.
items.explanation: Packing helps make the resulting layout useful rather than leaving islands arbitrarily placed.

items.title: Cast Modifier
items.fact: The Cast modifier shifts a mesh, curve, surface, or lattice toward a predefined sphere, cylinder, or cuboid shape.
items.explanation: It provides a procedural version of a shape-fitting operation.

items.title: Cast Sphere
items.fact: Cast can project geometry toward a spherical form.
items.explanation: This is useful for regularizing selected shapes toward a sphere.

items.title: Cast Cylinder
items.fact: Cast can project geometry toward a cylindrical form.
items.explanation: It can help reshape geometry toward cylindrical proportions.

items.title: Cast Cuboid
items.fact: Cast can project geometry toward a cuboid form.
items.explanation: This provides a box-like target shape for the deformation.

items.title: Cast and Smooth
items.fact: The Blender manual notes that Smooth can be a useful companion to Cast.
items.explanation: Smoothing can improve the appearance of a cast result or help address shading artifacts.

items.title: Apply Transform for Cast
items.fact: The Cast manual notes that applying transformations may be needed when the modified object looks wrong, especially for a cylinder cast.
items.explanation: The modifier uses local coordinates, so object transforms can affect its result.

items.title: Displace Modifier
items.fact: The Displace modifier moves mesh vertices based on the intensity of a texture.
items.explanation: A texture can therefore control procedural surface displacement.

items.title: Procedural Displacement
items.fact: Displace can use procedural textures.
items.explanation: Procedural data can shape a mesh without painting a displacement image.

items.title: Image Displacement
items.fact: Displace can use image textures.
items.explanation: An image can supply grayscale or vector information that controls vertex movement.

items.title: Displace Along Axis
items.fact: Displace can move vertices along a chosen local X, Y, or Z axis.
items.explanation: Axis displacement gives explicit directional control.

items.title: Displace Along Normal
items.fact: Displace can move vertices along their normals.
items.explanation: Normal-based displacement follows the local surface direction.

items.title: Vector Displacement
items.fact: The RGB components of a texture can drive local X, Y, and Z displacement simultaneously.
items.explanation: This is a form of vector displacement rather than a single scalar push.

items.title: Multires Sculpt Level
items.fact: The Multiresolution modifier can set a specific subdivision level for Sculpt Mode.
items.explanation: Artists can choose the resolution used while sculpting.

items.title: Decrease Multires Level
items.fact: `Alt`-`1` decreases the Multires sculpt level.
items.explanation: It switches to a lower subdivision level for broader work.

items.title: Increase Multires Level
items.fact: `Alt`-`2` increases the Multires sculpt level.
items.explanation: It switches to a higher subdivision level for finer detail.

items.title: Multires Render Level
items.fact: Multiresolution has a Render level setting.
items.explanation: The chosen render level controls subdivision shown when rendering.

items.title: Sculpt Base Mesh
items.fact: Sculpt Base Mesh can deform the unsubdivided base mesh while previewing the set sculpt level.
items.explanation: This supports broad changes while seeing higher-level details in context.

items.title: Avoid Surface Noise
items.fact: The Sculpt Base Mesh workflow is documented as a way to make broad changes without creating surface noise and artifacts.
items.explanation: Large edits can be made at the base level while preserving high-level visual context.

items.title: Optimal Display
items.fact: Optimal Display shows only edges of the original geometry.
items.explanation: It avoids drawing subdivided wire edges when visualizing the wireframe.

items.title: Catmull-Clark Subdivision
items.fact: Multires Subdivide provides smooth subdivision using Catmull-Clark by default.
items.explanation: Catmull-Clark generates a smoothed subdivision surface.

items.title: Simple Multires Subdivision
items.fact: Simple subdivision adds resolution without smoothing the base mesh edges.
items.explanation: It subdivides edges while retaining the unsmoothed shape.

items.title: Linear Multires Subdivision
items.fact: Linear subdivision uses linear interpolation of the sculpted displacement.
items.explanation: It provides a completely unsmoothed subdivision result.

items.title: Subdivision Surface Modifier
items.fact: The Subdivision Surface modifier splits the faces of a mesh into smaller faces, giving it a smooth appearance without permanently altering the original geometry.
items.explanation: This technique allows 3D artists to model using a simple, low-polygon shape while the software calculates and displays a high-resolution, smooth surface. It is a fundamental technique for modeling organic characters and smooth objects.

items.title: Blender's Subdivision Surface Modifier
items.fact: Blender's Subdivision Surface modifier splits the faces of a mesh into smaller faces to give it a smoother appearance, letting artists model with simple low-vertex meshes.
items.explanation: This modifier is non-destructive, meaning the underlying simple mesh, or 'control cage,' remains editable while the smoothed result is generated automatically.

items.title: Mesh Topology and Subdivision
items.fact: According to the Blender Manual, clean mesh topology matters greatly for the Subdivision Surface modifier, since adding edge loops lets an artist control where a subdivided surface looks sharp or smooth.
items.explanation: Without extra edge loops, applying the modifier to a simple shape like a cube can make it nearly unrecognizable, since the modifier smooths it aggressively by default.

items.title: Modifiers in Blender
items.fact: Modifiers are automatic operations that affect an object's geometry in a non-destructive way.
items.explanation: Modifiers allow artists to perform complex operations like subdivision surfaces, beveling, and mirroring without permanently changing the base geometry. This non-destructive workflow enables flexible editing and iteration.

items.title: Modifier
items.fact: A Blender modifier is an automatic operation that affects an object's geometry non-destructively.
items.explanation: The modifier changes the evaluated result without directly changing the base geometry.

items.title: Modifier Stack
items.fact: Several Blender modifiers can be combined into a Modifier Stack.
items.explanation: The stack applies a series of operations to one object.

items.title: Modifier Order
items.fact: Modifier order affects the final result.
items.explanation: Changing the order changes which result is passed from one operation to the next.

items.title: Top-to-Bottom Modifier Evaluation
items.fact: Blender calculates modifiers from the top of the stack downward.
items.explanation: An earlier modifier produces input for a later modifier.

items.title: Applying a Modifier
items.fact: Applying a modifier makes its effect permanent in the object data.
items.explanation: The live modifier is removed after its current result is committed.

items.title: Generate Modifiers
items.fact: Generate modifiers can change topology or add geometry.
items.explanation: They can construct new evaluated geometry from the original object.

items.title: Deform Modifiers
items.fact: Deform modifiers change an object's shape without altering its topology.
items.explanation: The same topology can produce a different evaluated shape.

items.title: Geometry Nodes Modifier
items.fact: Blender allows custom modifiers to be created through Geometry Nodes.
items.explanation: Node-based procedural systems can be used as object modifications.

items.title: Point Cloud
items.fact: A point cloud represents large numbers of individual points in 3D space.
items.explanation: It stores sparse spatial samples rather than requiring a connected surface mesh.

items.title: Point Cloud for Scan Data
items.fact: Point clouds are useful for visualizing 3D scan data.
items.explanation: Scanners can produce many spatial points that do not immediately need to be converted into a surface.

items.title: Point Cloud for Particles
items.fact: Point clouds can visualize particle simulation data.
items.explanation: Particles naturally correspond to collections of spatial points.

items.title: Point Cloud for Sparse Data
items.fact: Point clouds are useful for sparse datasets where a mesh surface is unnecessary or impractical.
items.explanation: Not every 3D dataset needs connected faces.

items.title: Point Attributes
items.fact: Point-cloud points can store attributes such as position and color.
items.explanation: Attributes add information to individual points beyond their location.

items.title: Point Cloud and Future Simulation
items.fact: Blender documents future plans to expand point-cloud support for systems such as particles.
items.explanation: The manual distinguishes current point-cloud representation from future system support.

items.title: Surface Object
items.fact: A Blender Surface is a smooth sheet defined by control points.
items.explanation: Surface objects provide mathematically defined smooth forms.

items.title: Surface Grid
items.fact: Surface control points are arranged in a grid with U and V directions.
items.explanation: The two directions define the surface parameterization.

items.title: Cyclic Surface
items.fact: A Surface can be open or closed in either or both directions.
items.explanation: Closing a direction can make forms such as cylinders or spheres.

items.title: Surface to Mesh
items.fact: A Surface can be converted to a mesh through Object Convert Mesh.
items.explanation: Conversion changes the representation to polygon mesh geometry.

items.title: NURBS Curve Primitive
items.fact: The Add Surface menu can add a NURBS Curve made from four control points forming an arc.
items.explanation: It provides a ready-made curve starting shape.

items.title: NURBS Circle Primitive
items.fact: The Add Surface menu can add a NURBS Circle.
items.explanation: It creates a closed loop of control points.

items.title: NURBS Surface Primitive
items.fact: The NURBS Surface primitive is a 4 by 4 control-point surface patch.
items.explanation: The center points are slightly raised in the default primitive.

items.title: NURBS Cylinder Primitive
items.fact: The NURBS Cylinder is an open cylinder made by extruding a NURBS Circle.
items.explanation: It provides a smooth surface-based cylinder starting point.

items.title: NURBS Sphere Primitive
items.fact: The NURBS Sphere is constructed from control points arranged in a cube-like structure.
items.explanation: The mathematical surface forms a sphere from the control arrangement.

items.title: NURBS Torus Primitive
items.fact: The NURBS Torus is created by rotating a circle around an axis.
items.explanation: It provides a doughnut-shaped surface primitive.

items.title: Add Menu Surface Shortcut
items.fact: The Add Surface menu is opened with `Shift`-`A`.
items.explanation: The Add menu is the standard entry point for adding scene primitives.

items.title: Text Geometry Offset
items.fact: Text Geometry Offset changes the control points of curves defining letters, making them thinner or thicker.
items.explanation: It modifies the outline of the letter curves.

items.title: Text Extrusion
items.fact: Text geometry supports extrusion.
items.explanation: Extrusion gives flat letter outlines three-dimensional depth.

items.title: Text Bevel
items.fact: Text geometry supports bevel settings.
items.explanation: Beveling softens or shapes the edges of extruded text.

items.title: Text Alignment
items.fact: The Paragraph panel controls text alignment.
items.explanation: Alignment affects how text is positioned relative to its frame or origin.

items.title: Left Alignment
items.fact: Left-aligned text starts at the left side of the frame or the object origin.
items.explanation: The text extends to the right from that reference.

items.title: Center Alignment
items.fact: Center alignment centers text within its frame or around the object origin.
items.explanation: The text grows equally to both sides around the center reference.

items.title: Right Alignment
items.fact: Right alignment places text against the right side of its frame or object-origin reference.
items.explanation: Text grows toward the left from that alignment point.

items.title: Justify Alignment
items.fact: Justify alignment flushes a line when it ends through word wrapping rather than a newline.
items.explanation: Whitespace is adjusted rather than character spacing alone.

items.title: Flush Alignment
items.fact: Flush alignment always flushes the line, even while typing.
items.explanation: It uses character spacing to fill lines.

items.title: Vertical Text Alignment
items.fact: Text objects support vertical alignment options such as top, middle, and bottom.
items.explanation: Vertical alignment controls where text sits within its reference frame.

items.title: Character Spacing
items.fact: Character spacing scales the space between characters.
items.explanation: It changes kerning-like spacing across the text.

items.title: Word Spacing
items.fact: Word spacing scales whitespace between words.
items.explanation: It adjusts gaps between words without changing character shapes.

items.title: Line Spacing
items.fact: Line spacing controls vertical spacing between text lines.
items.explanation: It changes the distance between successive lines.

items.title: Text Kerning Shortcut
items.fact: In Text Edit Mode, `Alt`-`Left` and `Alt`-`Right` change individual kerning.
items.explanation: This lets an artist adjust spacing at a specific text cursor position.

items.title: Texture Baking
items.fact: Baking creates a 2D bitmap image containing lighting, shadow, or geometry data calculated from a 3D scene.
items.explanation: Rendering complex lighting in real-time is expensive for a computer. Baking solves this by calculating the complex light bounces once and 'painting' those shadows directly onto the object's flat texture file, making the game run much faster.

items.title: Cycles Renderer in Blender
items.fact: Cycles is a physically based path tracing renderer in Blender.
items.explanation: Cycles produces highly realistic images by simulating how light behaves in the real world. It is typically used for final renders where photorealism is required, offering accurate lighting, materials, and shadows.

items.title: EEVEE Renderer in Blender
items.fact: EEVEE is a physically based real-time renderer in Blender.
items.explanation: EEVEE (Extra Easy Virtual Environment Engine) provides fast, interactive rendering suitable for real-time workflows. It is ideal for animations, previews, stylized rendering, and real-time feedback during scene setup.

items.title: Rendering Definition
items.fact: Rendering turns a 3D scene into a 2D image.
items.explanation: The renderer evaluates the scene from a camera and produces image output.

items.title: Three Built-In Engines
items.fact: Blender includes EEVEE, Cycles, and Workbench render engines.
items.explanation: Each engine targets different rendering workflows.

items.title: EEVEE Role
items.fact: EEVEE is a physically based realtime renderer focused on speed and interactivity.
items.explanation: It is useful for interactive viewport work and final renders where its feature set is appropriate.

items.title: Cycles Role
items.fact: Cycles is a physically based path tracer.
items.explanation: It calculates light transport using path-tracing methods.

items.title: Workbench Role
items.fact: Workbench is designed for layout, modeling, and previews.
items.explanation: It provides a fast visual feedback renderer for working scenes.

items.title: Third-Party Renderers
items.fact: Blender can use additional renderers supplied by third-party developers through add-ons.
items.explanation: The built-in engines are not the only rendering options available to a Blender installation.

items.title: Camera Lighting Materials
items.fact: The look of a render is defined by cameras, lights, and materials.
items.explanation: These scene elements determine what the renderer sees and how surfaces respond to light.

items.title: Shared Scene Concepts
items.fact: Cameras, lights, and materials are shared concepts between EEVEE and Cycles, although some features are engine-specific.
items.explanation: A scene can therefore often be previewed in both engines while respecting their differences.

items.title: Render Layers
items.fact: Blender can split renders into layers and passes.
items.explanation: This creates intermediate image information that can be recombined later.

items.title: Compositing in Blender
items.fact: Rendered layers and passes can be composited for creative control.
items.explanation: Compositing changes or combines rendered information after rendering.

items.title: Freestyle
items.fact: Freestyle can add non-photorealistic line rendering.
items.explanation: Line-based rendering can create stylized outlines and illustration-like effects.

items.title: Interactive Viewport Rendering
items.fact: Blender supports interactive 3D viewport rendering for all built-in render engines.
items.explanation: Interactive rendering helps artists iterate on lighting and shading before final output.

items.title: EEVEE Rasterization
items.fact: EEVEE is based on rasterization rather than being a path tracer.
items.explanation: Rasterization determines visible surfaces and then estimates lighting interactions with them.

items.title: EEVEE PBR
items.fact: EEVEE targets physically based rendering materials.
items.explanation: Its shader workflow is designed around PBR concepts even though it is not a path tracer.

items.title: EEVEE Material Compatibility
items.fact: EEVEE and Cycles use the same shader nodes for materials.
items.explanation: This makes EEVEE useful for previewing materials intended for Cycles.

items.title: Render Pass
items.fact: A render pass is intermediate rendering information extracted as a separate image.
items.explanation: Passes let artists access components of a render independently for compositing.

items.title: Depth Pass
items.fact: The Depth pass contains distance to the nearest visible surface.
items.explanation: Depth information can be used for effects such as compositing-based depth of field.

items.title: Mist Pass
items.fact: The Mist pass maps visible-surface distance to a 0.0–1.0 range.
items.explanation: This normalized depth-like signal can be used to create atmospheric or compositing effects.

items.title: Ambient Occlusion Pass
items.fact: Ambient Occlusion can be exported as a grayscale pass.
items.explanation: The values represent how occluded or exposed directly visible surfaces are.

items.title: Shadow Catcher Pass
items.fact: The Shadow Catcher pass contains shadows collected by shadow-catcher objects.
items.explanation: It can help composite rendered objects and shadows into recorded footage.

items.title: Shader AOV
items.fact: Shader AOV stands for Arbitrary Output Variable.
items.explanation: AOVs are custom render passes used to carry additional information into compositing.

items.title: AOV Color Type
items.fact: A Shader AOV can store Color data.
items.explanation: Color data can be used for colors, normals, or other vector information.

items.title: AOV Value Type
items.fact: A Shader AOV can store Value data.
items.explanation: Value data stores a single numeric quantity per pixel.

items.title: Light Groups
items.fact: Cycles supports Light Groups that produce combined passes illuminated by specific lights.
items.explanation: Multiple light-group passes can be combined during compositing to adjust individual light contributions.

items.title: Viewport Compositor Pass Support
items.fact: The viewport compositor supports render passes when using EEVEE; for other engines the passes are empty.
items.explanation: Engine choice therefore affects whether viewport compositing has pass data.

items.title: Blender Render Engine Comparison
items.fact: Blender includes three render engines with different strengths: EEVEE for real-time rendering, Cycles for physically based path tracing, and Workbench for basic shading.
items.explanation: EEVEE prioritizes performance and interactivity, Cycles focuses on physical accuracy and realism, and Workbench provides fast, simple shading options for modeling and layout work.

items.title: Node-Based Materials
items.fact: Blender materials, lights, and backgrounds can be defined with networks of shading nodes.
items.explanation: Nodes pass values, colors, vectors, and shaders between operations.

items.title: Shader Socket
items.fact: A shader socket carries a shader describing lighting interaction rather than simply a surface color.
items.explanation: The renderer uses shader information to determine how light interacts with a surface or volume.

items.title: BSDF Shader
items.fact: BSDF shaders describe reflection, refraction, and absorption at a surface.
items.explanation: They model how incoming light interacts with material surfaces.

items.title: Emission Shader
items.fact: An Emission shader describes light emission from a surface or volume.
items.explanation: It represents material-generated light rather than reflected light.

items.title: Volume Shader
items.fact: A Volume shader describes light scattering inside a volume.
items.explanation: Volume shading handles participating media within a volume.

items.title: Background Shader
items.fact: A Background shader describes light emission from the environment.
items.explanation: It defines environmental contribution surrounding the scene.

items.title: Mix Shader
items.fact: Shader nodes can be mixed using Mix Shader nodes.
items.explanation: Mixing lets different shader behaviors contribute to the resulting material.

items.title: Add Shader
items.fact: Shader nodes can be added using Add Shader nodes.
items.explanation: Adding combines shader contributions into a resulting shader.

items.title: Procedural Texture Nodes
items.fact: Blender includes built-in procedural texture nodes.
items.explanation: These nodes can generate texture-like values without requiring an external image.

items.title: Image Texture Node
items.fact: The Image Texture node is used for image-based UV mapping and texture painting.
items.explanation: It connects an image resource to the shader network.

items.title: Generated Coordinates
items.fact: Generated coordinates are the default texture coordinates for most nodes.
items.explanation: They provide an automatically generated coordinate space for procedural mapping.

items.title: Image Texture UV Default
items.fact: Image Texture nodes use UV coordinates by default.
items.explanation: This makes them suitable for image textures mapped through UV layouts.

items.title: Open Shading Language
items.fact: Cycles supports custom nodes written using Open Shading Language.
items.explanation: OSL provides a code-based route for custom shading operations in Cycles.

items.title: Principled BSDF
items.fact: The Principled BSDF node combines multiple layers into a single, easy-to-use shader based on Disney's physically-based rendering principles.
items.explanation: Rather than building complex materials from scratch using math, artists use sliders on the Principled BSDF—like 'Metallic', 'Roughness', and 'Base Color'—to realistically simulate almost any real-world material, from shiny plastic to rusted metal.

items.title: Normal Maps
items.fact: A Normal Map is a type of texture that fakes the lighting of bumps and dents on an otherwise flat polygon surface.
items.explanation: Instead of modeling thousands of individual tiny scales on a reptile, an artist can model a low-detail mesh and apply a Normal Map. The game engine uses the colors in the map to alter how light hits the flat surface, creating the illusion of 3D depth without the performance cost.

items.title: Workbench
items.fact: Blender's Workbench engine is optimized for fast rendering during modeling and animation preview.
items.explanation: It is designed for interactive work rather than slow final-quality rendering.

items.title: Workbench Not for Final Renders
items.fact: Blender states that Workbench is not intended as a final render engine for a project.
items.explanation: Its main purpose is viewport work and preview.

items.title: Workbench No Shader Nodes
items.fact: Workbench does not use shader nodes like EEVEE or Cycles.
items.explanation: Its shading is controlled through viewport and render settings instead.

items.title: Workbench Random Colors
items.fact: Workbench can assign random colors to objects.
items.explanation: Random coloring can help artists visually distinguish objects while modeling.

items.title: Workbench X-Ray
items.fact: Workbench has an X-ray mode.
items.explanation: X-ray allows parts of objects behind the front surface to be seen.

items.title: Workbench Cavity
items.fact: Workbench provides cavity shading.
items.explanation: Cavity shading can emphasize surface details useful during modeling.

items.title: Workbench Shadows
items.fact: Workbench supports shadow shading.
items.explanation: Shadows can help reveal form while inspecting a model.

items.title: Workbench Studio Lighting
items.fact: Workbench provides studio lighting.
items.explanation: Studio lighting gives a quick controlled illumination setup for inspecting objects.

items.title: Workbench MatCaps
items.fact: Workbench supports MatCaps.
items.explanation: MatCaps provide a predefined material and lighting appearance for viewport inspection.

items.title: Draw Brush
items.fact: Draw is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It is intended for adding or shaping surface volume.

items.title: Draw Sharp Brush
items.fact: Draw Sharp is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It provides a sharper style of surface deformation than the standard Draw brush.

items.title: Clay Brush
items.fact: Clay is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It provides a clay-like buildup workflow.

items.title: Clay Strips Brush
items.fact: Clay Strips is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It builds surfaces using strip-like strokes.

items.title: Inflate Brush
items.fact: Inflate is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It is designed for expanding surface regions.

items.title: Blob Brush
items.fact: Blob is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It creates localized bulging forms.

items.title: Crease Brush
items.fact: Crease is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It creates sharp recessed lines and grooves.

items.title: Smooth Brush
items.fact: Smooth is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It smooths surface irregularities.

items.title: Plane Brush
items.fact: Plane is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It is designed for flattening or planar surface work.

items.title: Pinch Brush
items.fact: Pinch is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It pulls surface detail inward to sharpen forms.

items.title: Grab Brush
items.fact: Grab is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It moves a broader region of the surface as a mass.

items.title: Elastic Deform
items.fact: Elastic Deform is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It provides elastic-style deformation of a surface region.

items.title: Snake Hook
items.fact: Snake Hook is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It pulls out long, hook-like forms from the surface.

items.title: Pose Brush
items.fact: Pose is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It supports posing-like deformation of sculpted forms.

items.title: Rotate Brush
items.fact: Rotate is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It rotates sculpted surface regions around the brush area.

items.title: Mask Brush
items.fact: Mask is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It paints a mask that restricts other sculpt operations.

items.title: Paint Brush
items.fact: Paint is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It applies color-related painting within sculpt workflows.

items.title: Blur Brush
items.fact: Blur is a sculpt brush type.
items.explanation: It blurs supported painted or surface information.

items.title: Brush Assets
items.fact: Blender provides default brush assets and preconfigured brush variants.
items.explanation: These built-in assets give artists practical starting settings.

items.title: Custom Brush Assets
items.fact: Custom brushes can be saved as assets.
items.explanation: Saving brushes as assets supports reuse across projects.

items.title: Brush Strength
items.fact: Brushes can be customized for strength.
items.explanation: Strength controls how strongly the brush affects its target.

items.title: Brush Falloff
items.fact: Brushes can be customized for falloff.
items.explanation: Falloff controls how influence changes across the brush radius.

items.title: Brush Texture Influence
items.fact: Brushes can be customized for texture influence.
items.explanation: Texture influence changes how a brush’s texture contributes to its effect.

items.title: Stroke Behavior
items.fact: Brushes can be customized for stroke behavior.
items.explanation: Stroke settings determine how brush movement translates into repeated effects.

items.title: Sculpt Mode Workflow
items.fact: Sculpt Mode changes a model primarily using brushes rather than individual vertices, edges, and faces.
items.explanation: The workflow is surface-oriented instead of component-oriented like Edit Mode.

items.title: Sculpt Mode Shortcut
items.fact: `Ctrl`-`Tab` can access the mode pie menu, including Sculpt Mode in supported contexts.
items.explanation: The mode menu provides a quick way to switch working modes.

items.title: Sculpt Brush Cursor
items.fact: In Sculpt Mode the cursor changes to a circle indicating brush size.
items.explanation: The circle shows the approximate area affected by the brush.

items.title: Apply Scale for Predictable Brushes
items.fact: Blender warns that applying mesh scale helps produce predictable brush behavior.
items.explanation: Unapplied object scale can affect how brush operations behave.

items.title: Sculpt Visibility
items.fact: Sculpt Mode includes visibility controls.
items.explanation: Visibility tools let artists isolate or hide parts of a model while sculpting.

items.title: Sculpt Masks
items.fact: Sculpt Mode supports masking.
items.explanation: Masks restrict where many sculpting operations can affect the model.

items.title: Face Sets
items.fact: Sculpt Mode supports Face Sets.
items.explanation: Face Sets organize regions of sculpted meshes for selective workflows.

items.title: Auto Masking
items.fact: Sculpt Mode provides auto-masking options.
items.explanation: Automatic masks can constrain brush influence based on mesh or selection properties.

items.title: Sculpt Filters
items.fact: Sculpt Mode provides filters.
items.explanation: Filters can modify larger regions of the sculpt rather than relying only on brush strokes.

items.title: Sculpt Transforming
items.fact: Sculpt Mode includes transformation operations.
items.explanation: Transform tools provide another way to reshape sculpted areas.

items.title: Sculpt Painting
items.fact: Sculpt Mode includes painting-related workflows.
items.explanation: Sculpting tools can be combined with painting and surface information.

items.title: Multiple Object Sculpting
items.fact: Blender documents working with multiple objects in sculpt workflows.
items.explanation: Artists can work across more than one sculptable object when supported.

items.title: Voxel Remesher
items.fact: Sculpting includes a Voxel Remesher option.
items.explanation: Voxel remeshing rebuilds geometry based on a voxel representation.

items.title: Dyntopo
items.fact: Sculpting includes Dynamic Topology, or Dyntopo.
items.explanation: It changes mesh tessellation dynamically during sculpting.

items.title: Multiresolution Sculpting
items.fact: Sculpting can use Multiresolution.
items.explanation: Multiresolution provides multiple subdivision levels for broad and detailed sculpt work.

items.title: Cloth Sculpting
items.fact: Blender has a Cloth Sculpting workflow.
items.explanation: Cloth tools can help shape and simulate cloth-like forms during sculpting.

items.title: Vertex Weights
items.fact: Vertex weights determine how much influence a specific bone has over a specific vertex on a 3D mesh.
items.explanation: When a character bends their knee, the geometry of the leg needs to bend with it. Assigning vertex weights (often through a process called weight painting) tells the software exactly which parts of the skin should stretch and move when the knee bone rotates.

items.title: One Root Node per Scene
items.fact: According to Godot's documentation, every scene is built as a hierarchy of nodes, and a scene always has exactly one root node.
items.explanation: This single-root structure is what allows scenes to be saved to disk, loaded again, and instanced as reusable building blocks inside other scenes.

items.title: Node
items.fact: Nodes are Godot's smallest building blocks.
items.explanation: Different node types provide different functions and can be combined into larger structures.

items.title: Scene
items.fact: A Godot scene can represent a character, weapon, door, user interface, or other game structure.
items.explanation: A scene packages a tree of nodes into a reusable unit.

items.title: Scene Tree
items.fact: Godot combines scenes into a scene tree.
items.explanation: The tree organizes the nodes that make up the running game.

items.title: Nested Scenes
items.fact: Godot scenes can be nested.
items.explanation: A saved scene can be inserted inside another scene as part of a larger structure.

items.title: Signal
items.fact: Godot nodes emit signals when events occur.
items.explanation: Signals provide an event-based way for nodes to notify other nodes.

items.title: Loose Coupling with Signals
items.fact: Godot signals allow nodes to communicate without hard-wiring them in code.
items.explanation: The sender does not need to directly depend on the receiver's implementation.

items.title: Built-In Signals
items.fact: Godot provides built-in signals for events such as collisions and area entry.
items.explanation: The engine can expose important events through the signal system.

items.title: Custom Signals
items.fact: Godot lets developers define new signals for their games.
items.explanation: Custom signals allow project-specific events to use the same communication pattern.

items.title: UI Scene
items.fact: Godot scenes can represent a user interface.
items.explanation: The scene system can structure menus and other interface elements.

items.title: Character Scene
items.fact: Godot's documentation gives characters as an example of what a scene can represent.
items.explanation: A character can therefore be packaged as a reusable scene structure.

items.title: Weapon Scene
items.fact: Godot's documentation gives weapons as an example of what a scene can represent.
items.explanation: A weapon can be built and reused as a scene.

items.title: Door Scene
items.fact: Godot's documentation gives doors as an example of what a scene can represent.
items.explanation: An interactive door can be organized as its own scene.

items.title: Node Name
items.fact: Every Godot node has a name.
items.explanation: Names identify nodes inside the scene tree.

items.title: Node Properties
items.fact: Godot nodes have editable properties.
items.explanation: Properties expose values that can be changed to configure a node.

items.title: Node Callbacks
items.fact: Godot nodes receive callbacks that can update every frame.
items.explanation: Callbacks give scripts defined points at which to react to engine updates.

items.title: Extending Nodes
items.fact: Godot nodes can be extended with new properties and functions.
items.explanation: Scripts can add project-specific behavior to the built-in node system.

items.title: Child Nodes
items.fact: Godot nodes can be added as children of other nodes.
items.explanation: Parent-child relationships form the hierarchy of a scene.

items.title: Scene Root
items.fact: A saved Godot scene has one root node.
items.explanation: The root is the top node from which the rest of the scene hierarchy descends.

items.title: Main Scene
items.fact: A Godot project has a main scene that is loaded first when the application runs.
items.explanation: The main scene serves as the starting point of the application.

items.title: 2D Scene Shortcut
items.fact: Godot's 2D Scene shortcut adds a Node2D root.
items.explanation: The shortcut provides a convenient starting structure for a 2D scene.

items.title: 3D Scene Shortcut
items.fact: Godot's 3D Scene shortcut adds a Node3D root.
items.explanation: The shortcut provides a convenient starting structure for a 3D scene.

items.title: UI Scene Shortcut
items.fact: Godot's User Interface shortcut adds a Control root.
items.explanation: The shortcut starts a UI-oriented scene with a Control node.

items.title: Godot Engine Overview
items.fact: Godot Engine is a feature-packed, cross-platform game engine to create 2D and 3D games from a unified interface.
items.explanation: Godot provides a comprehensive set of common tools so users can focus on making games without reinventing the wheel. It supports game development for desktop, mobile, web, and consoles from a single project.

items.title: Godot MIT License
items.fact: Godot is completely free and open source under the permissive MIT license with no royalties or usage restrictions.
items.explanation: The MIT license allows developers to use Godot for any purpose, including commercial projects, without paying fees or royalties. Users own their games completely, and the engine's development is fully independent and community-driven.

items.title: Godot Platform Export
items.fact: Games made with Godot can be exported with one click to major desktop, mobile, web, and console platforms.
items.explanation: Godot's export system streamlines the process of releasing games on multiple platforms. With a single project, developers can build versions for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, and the web.

items.title: SceneTree in Godot
items.fact: The SceneTree manages the hierarchy of nodes in a scene and the game loop in Godot.
items.explanation: As one of the most important classes in Godot, SceneTree manages nodes, handles scene switching, and controls the game loop. Nodes can be added, fetched, and removed, and the entire scene tree can be paused.

items.title: 3D Coordinates
items.fact: Godot's first 3D game tutorial teaches the use of 3D coordinates.
items.explanation: A 3D game represents positions in three spatial dimensions.

items.title: Jump Mechanic
items.fact: The tutorial implements jumping.
items.explanation: Jumping changes a character's vertical motion in response to gameplay logic.

items.title: Character Collision
items.fact: The tutorial uses kinematic-style character movement with collision detection.
items.explanation: Controlled character movement can still detect physical contact with the environment.

items.title: Physics Layers
items.fact: The tutorial uses physics layers to control which interactions are detected.
items.explanation: Layers let the physics system distinguish categories of objects for collision queries.

items.title: Procedural Monster Spawning
items.fact: The tutorial demonstrates instancing monsters at regular time intervals.
items.explanation: Code can generate repeated enemy instances while the game is running.

items.title: Runtime Animation Speed
items.fact: The tutorial demonstrates changing animation speed while the game runs.
items.explanation: Playback rate can be modified from gameplay logic.

items.title: 3D Game Interface
items.fact: The tutorial includes drawing a user interface over a 3D game.
items.explanation: A 3D game can combine world rendering with screen-space interface elements.

items.title: GDScript in Godot
items.fact: Godot uses GDScript as its primary scripting language, optimized for the engine with tight integration.
items.explanation: GDScript is a high-level, dynamically typed programming language designed specifically for Godot. Its syntax is similar to Python, making it accessible to beginners, while its tight integration with Godot's API allows for efficient game development.

items.title: Nodes in Godot
items.fact: Nodes are the basic building blocks in Godot and can be arranged in a tree structure called a scene.
items.explanation: Every game element in Godot is a Node. Nodes can be parented to other nodes, forming a tree hierarchy. A collection of nodes organized in this way is called a scene. Nodes communicate with each other using signals.

items.title: Signals in Godot
items.fact: Signals are Godot's implementation of the observer pattern, allowing nodes to communicate without directly referencing each other.
items.explanation: Signals are messages that nodes emit when specific events happen, like a button being pressed. Other nodes can connect to these signals and respond, which keeps code flexible and decoupled.

items.title: Scenes
items.fact: In Godot, a Scene is simply a collection of interconnected Nodes organized in a tree that has been saved to the disk.
items.explanation: Scenes are incredibly versatile. A scene can be a single bullet, a fully playable character, or an entire game level. Developers can instance scenes inside of other scenes, promoting highly modular game design.

items.title: The Node System
items.fact: In the Godot Engine, a Node is the fundamental building block for creating games, and all nodes are arranged in tree structures.
items.explanation: Everything in a Godot game is a Node or inherits from it. Nodes can execute logic, hold properties, and have child nodes, allowing developers to build complex scenes by snapping together simple, reusable components.

items.title: Observer Pattern
items.fact: Godot describes signals as its version of the observer pattern.
items.explanation: Signals allow one object to announce an event while other objects listen for it.

items.title: Button Press Signal
items.fact: Godot buttons can emit a signal when pressed.
items.explanation: A connected function can respond by performing an action such as opening a menu.

items.title: Timer for Cooldowns
items.fact: Godot's Timer node can be used for cooldowns and weapon reloading.
items.explanation: A timer can trigger logic after a chosen duration.

items.title: Signal Arguments
items.fact: Godot custom signals can carry declared arguments.
items.explanation: Arguments let an event send data along with the notification.

items.title: Code-Based Signal Connection
items.fact: Godot supports connecting signals through code.
items.explanation: This is useful when a connection needs to be established dynamically.

items.title: Ready Callback
items.fact: Godot's _ready callback runs when a node is fully instantiated.
items.explanation: It is a common location for initialization that depends on the node already existing.

items.title: Signals
items.fact: Godot uses a system called Signals to allow nodes to communicate with each other in a decoupled way by emitting notifications when specific events occur.
items.explanation: For example, a button node can emit a 'pressed' signal. Other nodes can connect to this signal and run specific code when the button is pressed, without the button needing to know anything about the nodes that are listening.

items.title: TileMaps
items.fact: The TileMap node allows developers to easily create grid-based 2D levels by painting tiles onto a map.
items.explanation: Instead of placing individual sprite nodes for every piece of ground in a platformer, developers set up a TileSet (a collection of images like grass, dirt, and rocks) and paint them rapidly across the screen, automatically handling grid alignment and collisions.

items.title: GDScript
items.fact: GDScript is Godot's built-in, dynamically typed scripting language designed specifically to integrate tightly with the engine's node architecture.
items.explanation: Modeled heavily after Python, GDScript uses indentation to define code blocks. It is highly optimized for Godot's math and object types, making it very fast to write and execute game logic.

items.title: Godot's Scene Tree
items.fact: In Godot, scenes are collections of nodes, and those nodes only become active once they enter the running Scene Tree.
items.explanation: Being part of the Scene Tree is what allows a node to process input, draw visuals, or receive notifications; nodes removed from the tree lose those abilities.

items.title: Recording Keyframes with Animation Record Mode
items.fact: Unity's Animation Record Mode lets a developer move a playback head to a chosen time and change a GameObject's properties, and Unity automatically saves those changes as new keyframes at that time.
items.explanation: This workflow means an animator doesn't need to manually insert every keyframe; simply changing a value while recording is enough to create one.

items.title: Audio Mixer Snapshots
items.fact: Unity Audio Mixer Snapshots capture the values of every parameter in a mixer at a given moment, and a game can transition between different snapshots at runtime.
items.explanation: This lets a game smoothly change its overall sound mix, for example muffling music and effects when a player pauses the game or enters underwater.

items.title: The Unity Audio Mixer
items.fact: Unity's Audio Mixer is an asset that Audio Sources can route through to apply mixing, effects, and mastering via a tree of Audio Mixer Groups.
items.explanation: Instead of controlling every sound individually, developers organize sounds into groups (like music, dialogue, or effects) that share volume and effect settings.

items.title: Audio Formats Unity Can Import
items.fact: Unity can import audio assets in AIFF, WAV, MP3, and Ogg file formats, treating them the same way it treats other project assets.
items.explanation: Supporting several common formats gives sound designers flexibility in how they deliver assets to a Unity project.

items.title: Pre-Build Callback
items.fact: Unity's BuildPlayerProcessor can add files and perform custom setup before a build starts.
items.explanation: Pre-build processing can prepare data needed by a project before packaging.

items.title: OnPreprocessBuild
items.fact: Unity supports an OnPreprocessBuild callback that runs at the start of a build.
items.explanation: It provides a defined hook for build-start preparation.

items.title: OnPostprocessBuild
items.fact: Unity supports an OnPostprocessBuild callback that runs at the end of a build.
items.explanation: It provides a hook for actions that should occur after packaging finishes.

items.title: Assembly Filtering
items.fact: Unity's IFilterBuildAssemblies callback can remove assemblies from a build.
items.explanation: Filtering lets a build process control which assemblies are included in the final output.

items.title: Build Pipeline
items.fact: Unity's build pipeline transforms a project into Player builds for target platforms.
items.explanation: The pipeline is the sequence of processes that converts project content into a runnable platform build.

items.title: Custom Build Script
items.fact: Unity lets developers customize builds with custom scripts.
items.explanation: A build script can automate project-specific preparation or packaging work.

items.title: Build Callbacks
items.fact: Unity lets developers customize the build process with callbacks.
items.explanation: Callbacks provide defined points where custom code can run during a build.

items.title: Command-Line Build
items.fact: Unity can build Players from the command line without opening the Editor.
items.explanation: Command-line builds make automation possible in build machines and development pipelines.

items.title: Platform Build Path
items.fact: Unity documents platform-specific build file extensions and path requirements.
items.explanation: Different platforms can require different output naming or path conventions.

items.title: Input
items.fact: Unity input is the mechanism by which a physical device sends a signal into a game or application.
items.explanation: Input lets a program receive actions from devices such as controllers, keyboards, mice, and touch screens.

items.title: Gamepad Input
items.fact: Unity supports gamepad input.
items.explanation: A gamepad can provide directional and button controls to a Unity application.

items.title: Mouse Input
items.fact: Unity supports mouse input.
items.explanation: Mouse events can be used for interface interaction or game controls.

items.title: Keyboard Input
items.fact: Unity supports keyboard input.
items.explanation: Keyboard keys can be used to control a character, navigate menus, or trigger actions.

items.title: Touch Input
items.fact: Unity supports touchscreen input.
items.explanation: Touch input allows a mobile application to respond to touches on the screen.

items.title: VR Controllers
items.fact: Unity supports VR controller input.
items.explanation: VR projects can receive input from supported virtual-reality controllers.

items.title: AR Controllers
items.fact: Unity supports AR controller input.
items.explanation: AR applications can use supported controller input as part of an interaction system.

items.title: Input System Package
items.fact: Unity provides the Input System package as a newer alternative to the classic input API.
items.explanation: The Input System package is intended to provide a more extensible and customizable input workflow.

items.title: Legacy Input Manager
items.fact: Unity retains a legacy Input Manager for older projects.
items.explanation: The legacy system remains available when compatibility with older input workflows is needed.

items.title: Input Actions
items.fact: The Unity Input System uses Actions as part of its input configuration workflow.
items.explanation: An action represents an input meaning such as movement or jumping rather than forcing game code to care about one particular device button.

items.title: Device Independence
items.fact: Unity's Input System can separate game input from particular devices.
items.explanation: The same gameplay action can be mapped to different controls on different devices.

items.title: UI Input
items.fact: Unity input is commonly used to let users navigate interfaces.
items.explanation: Menus and other UI elements need an input pathway so users can select and activate controls.

items.title: Character Control Input
items.fact: Unity describes input as necessary for controlling characters in games.
items.explanation: A character controller can translate a player's device input into in-game movement.

items.title: Object Interaction Input
items.fact: Unity identifies input as a way to move and interact with objects in virtual reality.
items.explanation: XR input can become the bridge between a physical controller action and an interaction in the virtual world.

items.title: Baked Light
items.fact: Unity's Baked light mode stores direct and indirect light in lightmaps.
items.explanation: The lighting is calculated before runtime and stored as texture data.

items.title: Realtime Light
items.fact: Unity's Realtime light mode generates direct light and shadows at runtime rather than baking them into lightmaps.
items.explanation: Realtime lighting is appropriate when lighting needs to respond while the game runs.

items.title: Baked Indirect Mode
items.fact: Unity's Baked Indirect mode combines realtime direct lighting with baked indirect lighting.
items.explanation: Direct illumination can remain dynamic while indirect illumination is precomputed.

items.title: Shadowmask Mode
items.fact: Unity's Shadowmask mode combines realtime direct lighting and baked indirect lighting with baked shadows in a shadowmask.
items.explanation: It mixes runtime lighting with stored shadow information.

items.title: Subtractive Mode
items.fact: Unity's Subtractive mode provides baked direct and indirect lighting and realtime direct shadows from one directional light.
items.explanation: The mode uses a more restricted dynamic shadowing arrangement.

items.title: UI Systems
items.fact: Unity currently supports UI Toolkit, Unity UI, and IMGUI.
items.explanation: These are Unity's three documented UI systems for creating interfaces in the editor and in applications.

items.title: UI Toolkit
items.fact: UI Toolkit is Unity's newer UI system.
items.explanation: It is designed for editor extensions and runtime UI.

items.title: UI Toolkit Web-Inspired Assets
items.fact: UI Toolkit uses resource types inspired by web formats such as XML and CSS.
items.explanation: The format provides a structured way to describe and style interface elements.

items.title: Retained-Mode UI
items.fact: UI Toolkit includes a retained-mode UI system.
items.explanation: In a retained-mode interface, the system maintains a representation of the UI elements instead of rebuilding the entire interface on every draw call.

items.title: Editor Extensions
items.fact: UI Toolkit can be used to create Unity Editor extensions.
items.explanation: The same UI technology can build tools inside the editor as well as runtime interfaces.

items.title: Runtime UI
items.fact: UI Toolkit can create runtime UI for games and applications.
items.explanation: A project can use UI Toolkit for interfaces that appear while the application is running.

items.title: AudioSource
items.fact: Unity's AudioSource represents an audio source in 3D.
items.explanation: Attach an AudioSource to a GameObject to play sounds in a 3D environment.

items.title: 3D Audio Listener
items.fact: To hear 3D AudioSource playback, Unity also requires an AudioListener.
items.explanation: The listener represents the point from which 3D audio is heard.

items.title: Audio as Component
items.fact: AudioSource is attached to a GameObject.
items.explanation: This connects the sound source to an object in the scene.

items.title: Canvas
items.fact: A Unity Canvas is an element that can be used for screen rendering.
items.explanation: UI elements placed on a Canvas can be rendered as part of the application's interface.

items.title: Canvas Render Timing
items.fact: Canvas elements are rendered after scene rendering.
items.explanation: This ordering allows screen UI to be drawn after the normal 3D or 2D scene output.

items.title: Camera Canvas Rendering
items.fact: Canvas elements can be rendered from an attached camera.
items.explanation: A camera can be involved in the rendering of a Canvas depending on its render mode.

items.title: Overlay Canvas
items.fact: Unity supports an overlay rendering mode for Canvas UI.
items.explanation: Overlay UI can be rendered independently of normal scene depth.

items.title: CanvasGroup
items.fact: CanvasGroup can modify child alpha, raycasting, and enabled state.
items.explanation: A CanvasGroup can affect a group of UI elements together.

items.title: CanvasRenderer
items.fact: CanvasRenderer renders to the screen after normal rendering when attached to a Canvas.
items.explanation: It participates in Unity's Canvas-based UI drawing path.

items.title: RectTransformUtility
items.fact: Unity provides RectTransformUtility helper methods for working with RectTransform objects.
items.explanation: The utility class provides code support for common rectangular UI-coordinate operations.

items.title: Kinematic Rigidbody
items.fact: Setting Rigidbody.isKinematic true prevents forces, collisions, and joints from affecting the Rigidbody directly.
items.explanation: The body is instead controlled by animation or script through transform changes.

items.title: Animation-Driven Physics
items.fact: A kinematic Rigidbody can be controlled by animation.
items.explanation: This is useful for characters or objects whose motion comes from animation rather than free physics.

items.title: Script-Driven Kinematic Body
items.fact: A kinematic Rigidbody can be controlled by script.
items.explanation: Code can set its movement while the physics system still treats it as a kinematic body.

items.title: Kinematic Collision Influence
items.fact: Kinematic rigidbodies can affect the motion of other rigidbodies through collisions or joints.
items.explanation: A kinematic object can therefore drive interactions even though external forces do not drive it.

items.title: Ragdoll Switching
items.fact: Unity documents changing isKinematic as a way to switch a character between animation-driven movement and ragdoll physics.
items.explanation: A character can normally follow animation and temporarily hand control to physics.

items.title: Rigidbody
items.fact: A Rigidbody is a Unity component that controls an object's position through physics simulation.
items.explanation: Adding a Rigidbody places the object's motion under Unity's physics engine.

items.title: Rigidbody Forces
items.fact: A Rigidbody can be affected by the physics engine rather than being moved only by ordinary transform changes.
items.explanation: Physics simulation can determine motion from forces and collisions.

items.title: MovePosition
items.fact: Rigidbody.MovePosition moves a kinematic Rigidbody toward a position.
items.explanation: It is designed for moving a Rigidbody through the physics system.

items.title: MoveRotation
items.fact: Rigidbody.MoveRotation rotates a Rigidbody.
items.explanation: Code can use it to move rotational state through the physics workflow.

items.title: Rigidbody Sleep
items.fact: A Rigidbody can be forced to sleep until it is woken.
items.explanation: Sleeping lets the physics system temporarily stop actively simulating an inactive body.

items.title: Rigidbody Wake
items.fact: Rigidbody.WakeUp forces a sleeping body to wake.
items.explanation: The body can be returned to active physics simulation when needed.

items.title: Sweep Test
items.fact: Rigidbody.SweepTest checks whether a Rigidbody would collide if moved through the Scene.
items.explanation: It is a predictive collision query rather than an actual move.

items.title: Collision Enter Callback
items.fact: OnCollisionEnter is called when a collider or Rigidbody begins touching another collider or Rigidbody.
items.explanation: A script can react to the start of a collision using this callback.

items.title: Collision Exit Callback
items.fact: OnCollisionExit is called when contact with another collider or Rigidbody ends.
items.explanation: A script can use the callback to respond when two objects stop touching.

items.title: Collision Stay Callback
items.fact: OnCollisionStay is called once per frame for each contact that continues.
items.explanation: It can support logic that needs to run while two physics objects remain in contact.

items.title: Render Pipeline Choice
items.fact: Unity's lighting workflow begins by choosing a render pipeline.
items.explanation: The selected pipeline affects which lighting features and customization options are available.

items.title: Built-in Render Pipeline
items.fact: Unity documents the Built-in Render Pipeline as not scriptable.
items.explanation: It differs from the scriptable render-pipeline options in how rendering is configured.

items.title: URP
items.fact: Unity documents the Universal Render Pipeline as a render pipeline option.
items.explanation: URP is one of Unity's supported rendering paths.

items.title: HDRP
items.fact: Unity documents the High Definition Render Pipeline as a render pipeline option.
items.explanation: HDRP is a Unity rendering path intended for high-fidelity graphics workflows.

items.title: Custom SRP
items.fact: Unity allows a Custom Scriptable Render Pipeline to be selected.
items.explanation: A project can build on Unity's scriptable rendering architecture when built-in pipeline behavior is not enough.

items.title: Baked GI
items.fact: Unity provides baked global illumination as a lighting workflow choice.
items.explanation: Light information can be precomputed rather than fully recalculated at runtime.

items.title: Realtime GI
items.fact: Unity provides realtime global illumination as a lighting workflow choice.
items.explanation: Indirect lighting can be updated while the scene runs when supported by the selected setup.

items.title: Mixed GI
items.fact: Unity allows a mixed baked and realtime global-illumination workflow.
items.explanation: A scene can combine precomputed and dynamic contributions.

items.title: Reflection Probes
items.fact: Unity's lighting workflow supports reflection probes.
items.explanation: Reflection probes provide captured reflection information that can contribute to scene rendering.

items.title: Light Probes
items.fact: Unity's lighting workflow can use Light Probes when a GI mode is selected.
items.explanation: Light probes provide lighting information for dynamic objects in supported workflows.

items.title: Unity Player
items.fact: When Unity creates a build of an application, it creates a Player.
items.explanation: A Player is the platform-specific runtime application generated from the Unity project.

items.title: Build Profiles
items.fact: Unity uses build profiles to configure builds for different platforms.
items.explanation: A build profile holds platform-specific build configuration that can be selected for packaging.

items.title: Platform-Specific Build
items.fact: Unity's build process supports creating application Players for different target platforms.
items.explanation: The same project can be prepared for multiple platforms through appropriate build configuration.

items.title: Incremental Build
items.fact: Unity documents incremental building as part of its build process.
items.explanation: An incremental build can reuse work that does not need to be rebuilt, reducing unnecessary processing.

items.title: CI Builds
items.fact: Unity documents command-line Player builds as useful for continuous-integration systems and build pipelines.
items.explanation: Automated build servers can invoke Unity without requiring a person to open the Editor.

items.title: Build Target Argument
items.fact: Unity uses the -buildTarget argument to select a target platform for a command-line build.
items.explanation: The argument tells the build process which platform configuration to use.

items.title: Active Build Profile Argument
items.fact: Unity uses -activeBuildProfile to select a saved build profile for a command-line build.
items.explanation: A saved profile can provide the configuration for an automated build.

items.title: Batch Mode
items.fact: Unity's -batchmode option runs the Editor without a graphical user interface.
items.explanation: Batch mode is suitable for automation where interactive editor windows are unnecessary.

items.title: Project Path Argument
items.fact: Unity requires -projectPath for command-line builds.
items.explanation: The argument identifies which project the build process should operate on.

items.title: Quit After Build
items.fact: Unity documents -quit as a required argument for command-line builds.
items.explanation: It tells the Editor to exit after the command-line operation completes.

items.title: IL2CPP Conversion
items.fact: Unity documents IL2CPP as converting C# code and assemblies to C++ before producing target-platform binaries.
items.explanation: The build process transforms managed project code into C++ as part of IL2CPP compilation.

items.title: IL2CPP Build Output
items.fact: Unity uses the IL2CPP pipeline to generate target-platform binary files.
items.explanation: The end result is a platform-specific runtime built from the converted code.

items.title: Scripting Backend
items.fact: Unity can choose a scripting backend for building an application.
items.explanation: The scripting backend is part of how Unity turns project scripts into a platform runtime.

items.title: Mono Backend
items.fact: Unity documents Mono as one of its scripting backend options.
items.explanation: Mono is one of the back-end choices available through Player Settings.

items.title: IL2CPP Backend
items.fact: Unity documents IL2CPP as one of its scripting backend options.
items.explanation: IL2CPP is another back-end choice available during application configuration.

items.title: Backend Configuration
items.fact: Unity lets users change the scripting backend through Player Settings.
items.explanation: Backend selection is treated as a build configuration rather than a change to gameplay code itself.

items.title: Animator
items.fact: Unity's Animator component provides an interface for controlling the Mecanim animation system.
items.explanation: It is the runtime component used to control a character's animation state and related behavior.

items.title: Avatar
items.fact: Animator exposes an Avatar associated with the current animated character.
items.explanation: An Avatar represents the mapping of a humanoid character to Unity's animation system.

items.title: Root Motion
items.fact: Animator exposes an applyRootMotion property.
items.explanation: Root motion lets animation data influence an object's movement when the workflow is configured to use it.

items.title: Animated Physics
items.fact: Animator has an animatePhysics option for interaction with physics and kinematic Rigidbodies.
items.explanation: The setting controls whether physics uses animated transforms in that situation.

items.title: Animation Culling
items.fact: Animator has a cullingMode property.
items.explanation: Culling controls how animation evaluation is handled when the animated object is not visible under the chosen culling policy.

items.title: Animator Controller
items.fact: The Animator Controller allows you to arrange and maintain a set of Animation Clips and associated Animation Transitions for a character or object.
items.explanation: Using a visual node-based state machine, developers can define when a character should switch from a 'walking' animation to a 'jumping' animation based on specific conditions, such as pressing a button or changing speed.

items.title: Audio Mixer
items.fact: The Audio Mixer allows you to route various audio sources through custom processing and effects before outputting them to the listener.
items.explanation: Instead of playing every sound effect directly to the player's speakers, developers can group sounds into categories (like 'Music', 'Dialogue', or 'Effects') in the Audio Mixer. This makes it easy to adjust the volume of all sound effects at once or apply effects like echoes to a specific group.

items.title: Raycasting
items.fact: A Raycast conceptually projects an invisible line through 3D space to detect collisions with objects in its path.
items.explanation: Raycasting is commonly used for shooting mechanics, line-of-sight checks for AI, or determining what object the player clicked on. The system returns information about the object hit, including the exact coordinate of the impact.

items.title: Audio Source Component in Unity
items.fact: An Audio Source component is attached to a GameObject to control how and where sounds play in a Unity scene.
items.explanation: Audio Source components are essential for integrating sound effects, music, and commentary into a game. By attaching an Audio Source to a GameObject, developers can control playback properties like volume, pitch, and 3D spatial positioning.

items.title: Rigidbodies
items.fact: Adding a Rigidbody component to an object puts its motion under the control of Unity's physics engine.
items.explanation: Once a Rigidbody is attached, the object will automatically respond to gravity, mass, drag, and collisions. This means the developer does not have to manually script the math for falling or bouncing.

items.title: ScriptableObjects
items.fact: A ScriptableObject is a data container that you can use to save large amounts of data, independent of class instances.
items.explanation: Instead of storing data like the stats of a sword (damage, weight, cost) inside the sword object itself—which duplicates data if there are 100 swords in the game—a ScriptableObject stores those stats in a single shared file that all swords reference, saving massive amounts of memory.

items.title: Coroutines
items.fact: A coroutine is a function that can suspend its execution until a given YieldInstruction finishes.
items.explanation: Unlike standard functions that execute their entire block of code in a single frame, coroutines allow you to pause execution and resume it in subsequent frames. This is highly useful for creating time-based effects, like fading out a color over several seconds.

items.title: GameObjects in Unity
items.fact: The GameObject is the fundamental object in Unity scenes, representing characters, props, scenery, cameras, and waypoints.
items.explanation: Every object in a Unity game is a GameObject. However, a GameObject cannot do anything on its own; it acts as a container for Components, which define its functionality.

items.title: Components in Unity
items.fact: A GameObject's functionality is defined by the Components attached to it.
items.explanation: Components are the functional pieces that give a GameObject its properties and behaviors. Unity has many built-in components like Transform, Light, and Rigidbody, and developers can create custom components using scripts.

items.title: Transform Component in Unity
items.fact: A GameObject always has a Transform component attached to represent its position, rotation, and scale.
items.explanation: The Transform component is essential for every GameObject in Unity. It defines where the object is located in the game world, how it is oriented, and its size. This component cannot be removed from a GameObject.

items.title: Unity Scripting API
items.fact: Unity allows developers to create their own components using the Unity Scripting API.
