items.explanation: By writing scripts that inherit from MonoBehaviour, developers can create custom behaviors and functionality for GameObjects. This scripting API provides access to Unity's extensive features and allows for complex game logic.

items.title: Navigation Mesh (NavMesh)
items.fact: The Navigation system in Unity uses a NavMesh, which is a data structure describing the walkable surfaces of the game world for artificial intelligence agents.
items.explanation: A NavMesh is generated based on the level's geometry. AI characters use this mesh to calculate paths from their current location to a destination, allowing them to navigate complex terrain and avoid obstacles automatically.

items.title: Occlusion Culling
items.fact: Occlusion culling is a process which prevents Unity from performing rendering calculations for GameObjects that are completely hidden from view by other GameObjects.
items.explanation: If a player is standing in front of a massive wall, the engine doesn't need to draw the forest behind it. Occlusion culling calculates these blocked sightlines and turns off the hidden objects to save processing power.

items.title: Prefabs
items.fact: A Prefab acts as a template from which you can create new object instances in a Unity scene.
items.explanation: Prefabs allow developers to create, configure, and store a game object complete with all its components and properties. Any edits made to a Prefab asset are immediately reflected in all instances of that Prefab across the project, saving time and ensuring consistency.

items.title: The Canvas
items.fact: The Canvas is the area that all UI elements should be inside, acting as the root component for rendering User Interfaces in Unity.
items.explanation: Every button, text box, or image on a game's interface must be a child of a Canvas. The Canvas handles how these elements are drawn to the screen, whether they sit flat on the camera lens or exist as physical panels inside the 3D world.

items.title: Joints Are the Building Blocks of a Maya Skeleton
items.fact: In Maya, joints are the fundamental building blocks of a skeleton and its points of articulation; joints have no shape of their own and cannot be rendered.
items.explanation: Because joints are invisible in a final render, riggers rely on the visible mesh that is bound to the skeleton to see the effect of joint movement.

items.title: Bones Are Visual Aids, Not Real Objects
items.fact: Maya's documentation explains that bones, the lines drawn between joints, are only visual cues showing the relationship between joints and have no physical or calculable presence in the scene.
items.explanation: This distinction matters because it's the joints, not the bones themselves, that actually drive deformation when a character rig is animated.

items.title: ACM SIGGRAPH and Computer Graphics Education
items.fact: ACM SIGGRAPH is the ACM Special Interest Group for Computer Graphics and Interactive Techniques, supporting educators and learners in these fields.
items.explanation: SIGGRAPH is the leading professional organization for computer graphics and interactive techniques. Its Education Committee develops curriculum guidelines, offers instructional resources, and organizes activities to foster excellence in computer graphics education worldwide.

items.title: SIGGRAPH Educational Resources
items.fact: The ACM SIGGRAPH Education Committee provides global online resources for educators to help define a knowledge base for the discipline.
items.explanation: These resources include curriculum guidelines, instructional materials, and innovative learning tools. The committee works to identify core competencies, support educational projects, and connect education communities.

items.title: glTF as a 3D Asset Delivery Format
items.fact: glTF (GL Transmission Format) is a royalty-free specification created by the Khronos Group for efficiently transmitting and loading 3D scenes and models in applications.
items.explanation: glTF is designed to minimize both the file size of 3D assets and the amount of processing needed to unpack and use them at runtime.

items.title: HumanIK
items.fact: Autodesk HumanIK is described as a full-body inverse-kinematics solver and retargeter.
items.explanation: It can solve body poses and transfer animation between character structures.

items.title: HumanIK Keyframing
items.fact: Maya HumanIK provides a full-body and body-part keyframing environment.
items.explanation: Animators can key and manipulate full bodies or selected body parts.

items.title: HumanIK Effectors
items.fact: HumanIK provides auxiliary effectors and pivots.
items.explanation: Effectors provide controls that influence the solved character pose.

items.title: HumanIK Pinning
items.fact: HumanIK includes pinning.
items.explanation: Pinning can hold selected character controls in place while solving other parts of the body.

items.title: HumanIK Retargeting
items.fact: HumanIK can retarget animation between characters of different size, proportions, and skeletal hierarchy.
items.explanation: A retargeting system maps motion from one character structure to another.

items.title: HumanIK Character Setup
items.fact: Each character used in HumanIK retargeting must be set up as a HumanIK character.
items.explanation: The system needs a recognized HumanIK character definition for retargeting.

items.title: Maya Character Setup
items.fact: Autodesk describes character setup as involving rigging before animation.
items.explanation: A character is prepared with systems that make animation practical.

items.title: Skeletons in Maya
items.fact: Maya character rigging can include creating skeletons.
items.explanation: A skeleton provides joints and bones used to control character motion.

items.title: IK Handles
items.fact: Maya character rigging can include IK handles.
items.explanation: Inverse-kinematics handles provide control over chains of joints.

items.title: Skin Binding
items.fact: Maya character setup can bind skins to skeletons.
items.explanation: Binding connects character geometry to the skeleton so bone motion can deform it.

items.title: Deformers
items.fact: Maya supports deformers for animation.
items.explanation: Deformers can change an object's shape based on controlled parameters or relationships.

items.title: Constraints
items.fact: Maya character setup can use constraints.
items.explanation: Constraints limit or control the transformations of animated objects.

items.title: Jiggle Deformer
items.fact: Autodesk gives a jiggle deformer as an example of creating a secondary deformation effect.
items.explanation: A deformer can produce localized motion such as a soft-body jiggle.

items.title: Wire Deformer
items.fact: Autodesk gives a wire deformer as an example of character deformation.
items.explanation: A wire can influence geometry to produce a controlled shape change.

items.title: Lattice Deformer
items.fact: Autodesk gives a lattice deformer as an example of character deformation.
items.explanation: A lattice can bend or reshape the geometry inside a deforming volume.

items.title: Maya Dynamics
items.fact: Maya can use dynamics such as particle emitters, fields, and fluids in animation setups.
items.explanation: Dynamic simulation systems can be constrained to scene objects or characters.

items.title: Custom Rig Mapping
items.fact: Maya can map a custom rig for source animation streaming from MotionBuilder or HumanIK.
items.explanation: A mapping tells the system how a custom rig corresponds to an animation structure.

items.title: Skeleton Definition
items.fact: A valid skeleton definition is required for a custom rig mapping.
items.explanation: The mapping process needs a defined skeletal structure before animation can be assigned.

items.title: Custom Rig Controllers
items.fact: Maya's Custom Rig tab can map custom rig controllers to corresponding effectors.
items.explanation: Controllers are assigned to the rig structures that represent their animation functions.

items.title: Controller Tag
items.fact: Maya can tag objects as controllers.
items.explanation: Controller tags identify scene objects that are intended to control animation.

items.title: Controller Visibility
items.fact: Controller tags can control visibility based on mouse proximity.
items.explanation: The rig display can be made less visually cluttered by changing controller visibility.

items.title: Pickwalk Hierarchy
items.fact: Controller tags can define custom pickwalk hierarchies.
items.explanation: Animators can navigate through related controls according to an authored hierarchy.

items.title: Controller Display
items.fact: Maya can show controller nodes in Viewport 2.0.
items.explanation: The viewport can display the objects identified as animation controllers.

items.title: Graph Editor in Maya
items.fact: The Graph Editor in Maya graphically represents animated attributes as animation curves.
items.explanation: The Graph Editor displays how attribute values change over time using curves. Animators can refine motion by adjusting the shape of these curves, changing key positions, and adding or removing keys to achieve the desired timing and feel.

items.title: Keyframe Animation in Maya
items.fact: Keyframe animation in Maya lets you transform objects or skeletons over time by setting keyframes.
items.explanation: Animators set keys that represent when the attributes of an object change. Between these keyframes, Maya automatically interpolates the motion, creating smooth animation. For example, keyframing a character's arm joints creates an animation of the arm waving.

items.title: Setting Keyframes in Maya
items.fact: To set a keyframe in Maya, animators select an object, move the Time Slider, set an attribute value, and place a key using the S hotkey.
items.explanation: This process takes a snapshot of the attribute's value at that moment in time. Animators can set more precise values using the Attribute Editor, Channel Box, or Graph Editor. Keyframes can be rearranged, removed, duplicated, and stretched.

items.title: Driven Key Animation in Maya
items.fact: Driven key animation in Maya lets you link and drive the attributes of one object with those of another.
items.explanation: This technique uses one object's attributes (drivers) to control another object's attributes (driven). For example, a character's movement can drive the rotation of a door, creating interactive animations.

items.title: Nonlinear Animation in Maya
items.fact: Nonlinear animation in Maya allows animators to split, duplicate, and blend animation clips.
items.explanation: This technique enables animators to create and reuse animation clips, such as walk cycles, and blend them together to achieve complex motion effects without starting from scratch.

items.title: Path Animation in Maya
items.fact: Path animation in Maya allows animators to set a curve as an animation path for an object.
items.explanation: When an object is attached to a motion path, it follows the curve during its animation. For example, a car model assigned to a motion path will follow the road in the scene.

items.title: Motion Capture Animation in Maya
items.fact: Motion capture animation in Maya allows animators to use imported motion capture data to apply realistic motion to characters.
items.explanation: Motion capture data records real-world movements, which can be applied to digital characters. For example, the captured motion of a horse can be used to animate the skeleton of a quadruped model.

items.title: Layered Animation in Maya
items.fact: Layered animation in Maya allows animators to create and blend animation on separate layers.
items.explanation: Animation layers let animators modify an animation sequence without permanently altering the original. This is useful for organizing complex animations and experimenting with variations.

items.title: Dynamic Animation in Maya
items.fact: Dynamic animation in Maya uses the rules of physics to simulate natural forces and create realistic motion.
items.explanation: Maya Dynamics can create effects such as sparks spraying from a welding torch or hail falling from the sky. This technique simulates physical behaviors like gravity, collisions, and wind.

items.title: Animation Expressions in Maya
items.fact: Expressions in Maya are instructions that animators can type to animate attributes.
items.explanation: Animation expressions are text-based formulas that control attribute values over time. For example, an expression can be written to animate the flapping of a bird's wings.

items.title: The Graph Editor
items.fact: The Graph Editor displays animation keys as points on a graph and represents the interpolation between them as mathematically adjustable curves.
items.explanation: Animators use the Graph Editor to fine-tune the speed and timing of an object's movement. By adjusting the handles on the curves, an animator can make a ball accelerate quickly and slow down smoothly without adding new keyframes.

items.title: Blend Shapes
items.fact: A blend shape deformer lets you change the shape of an object into the shapes of other target objects to create animation.
items.explanation: Often used for facial animation, a base face model can be morphed seamlessly into a target model shaped like a smile or a frown. The animator simply adjusts a slider to control how much influence the target shape has on the base shape.

items.title: Skinning
items.fact: Skinning is the process of binding a 3D deformable object (the skin) to a skeleton so that the object moves when the joints of the skeleton are posed.
items.explanation: Without skinning, a 3D character is just a rigid statue with bones floating inside it. Skinning links the polygon mesh to the bones, mathematically determining how the skin stretches and bends as the joints rotate.

items.title: NURBS Modeling
items.fact: NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) are mathematical representations of 3D geometry that can describe any shape from a simple 2D line to a highly complex 3D organic surface.
items.explanation: Unlike polygon modeling, which builds shapes using flat geometric faces, NURBS modeling uses mathematical curves to create perfectly smooth surfaces. It is heavily used in automotive design and industrial rendering where absolute precision is required.

items.title: Maya's Quick Rig Tool
items.fact: Maya's Quick Rig tool, accessed through the HumanIK window, lets an artist rig a biped character mesh automatically or by following a step-by-step guided workflow.
items.explanation: This tool speeds up character setup by aligning a skeleton's guides to a mesh automatically instead of requiring every joint to be placed by hand.

items.title: Audio Clip in Unity
items.fact: For an Audio Source to play sound, an Audio Clip must be added to it.
items.explanation: Audio Clips are the actual sound files (such as WAV or MP3) that contain the audio data. The Audio Source component references these clips and controls how they are played back in the game environment.

sources.title: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Minimum Viable Prototype
items.fact: Unity's production-plan tutorial defines an initial milestone as a minimum viable prototype.
items.explanation: The milestone focuses on having prototype versions of the core systems and critical player actions.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Core Systems in Prototype
items.fact: The minimum viable prototype should include prototype versions of the core systems.
items.explanation: Core systems are the systems necessary to demonstrate how the main game experience works.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Critical Player Actions
items.fact: The minimum viable prototype should include critical player actions.
items.explanation: The player actions that are essential to the game should be testable early rather than postponed until late production.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Feature Dependencies
items.fact: Unity instructs developers to identify dependencies or connections between prioritized features and systems.
items.explanation: A dependency means that one feature relies on another feature or system being available.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Milestone from GDD
items.fact: The production-plan tutorial says to review prioritized features in the game design document when defining a milestone.
items.explanation: The production plan can be derived from the priorities already established in the design document.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Prototype UI Dependency
items.fact: Unity gives an example where a core conversation system and its interface both need prototype implementations because the systems are connected.
items.explanation: A milestone may need multiple prototype pieces when one system cannot be meaningfully demonstrated without another.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Feature Prioritization
items.fact: Unity's production workflow includes prioritizing the features for the game before defining the first milestone.
items.explanation: Prioritization helps the team decide which features must be represented in early development work.

source.name: Unity Learn: Create your production plan

items.title: Unity's Timeline Infinite Clip
items.fact: In Unity's Timeline Editor, recording a keyframed animation directly on a GameObject creates a special clip called an Infinite Clip.
items.explanation: This differs from importing a pre-made animation from a 3D program; it's built by recording changes right inside the Timeline window.

items.title: Game Design Definition
items.fact: Unity's game design tutorial describes game design as distinct from simply building a game with an engine and code.
items.explanation: Game design concerns the rules, goals, challenges, feedback, and player experience that shape what a game is like to play.

items.title: Goals
items.fact: Unity identifies goals as a core building block of game design.
items.explanation: A goal gives the player something the game asks them to accomplish.

items.title: Rules
items.fact: Unity identifies rules as a core building block of game design.
items.explanation: Rules define the boundaries and conditions under which the game operates.

items.title: Mechanics
items.fact: Unity identifies mechanics as core game-design building blocks.
items.explanation: Mechanics are the systems and actions through which players interact with the game.

items.title: Challenge
items.fact: Unity identifies challenge as a core building block of game design.
items.explanation: Challenge represents the obstacles or difficulty the player must deal with.

items.title: Feedback
items.fact: Unity identifies feedback as a core building block of game design.
items.explanation: Feedback communicates the results of player actions so players can understand what happened.

items.title: Core Loop
items.fact: Unity explains that game-design elements combine into a core loop.
items.explanation: A core loop is the recurring pattern of actions and responses that forms a large part of moment-to-moment play.

items.title: Player Experience
items.fact: Unity explains that the core loop helps shape player experience.
items.explanation: The repeated interaction pattern contributes to how the game feels and plays over time.

items.title: Game Deconstruction
items.fact: Unity's tutorial asks learners to practice deconstructing a simple game.
items.explanation: Breaking a game into its goals, rules, mechanics, challenge, feedback, and loop can make its design easier to analyze.

items.title: Game Design Document
items.fact: Unity's game-design tutorial has learners fill out related parts of a game design document.
items.explanation: A GDD records intended game-design elements so they can be communicated and developed systematically.

items.title: Core Design Elements
items.fact: Unity organizes a GDD section around core design elements.
items.explanation: The design document can collect the foundational decisions that describe how a game should work.

items.title: Difficulty
items.fact: Unity's tutorial treats difficulty as part of putting together a game design.
items.explanation: Difficulty is a design variable that affects the challenges players encounter.

items.title: Game Feel
items.fact: Unity's tutorial includes game feel alongside the core loop, difficulty, and player experience.
items.explanation: Game feel concerns how the interaction and response of a game are experienced by the player.

items.title: Unity In-Editor Tutorial
items.fact: Unity includes a powerful in-Editor tutorial system that allows you to learn by doing, all within the Unity Editor.
items.explanation: This built-in learning system guides beginners through Unity's interface and tools using highlighted callouts and embedded instructions, eliminating the need to switch between a web browser and the editor.

items.title: Unity Hub Project Management
items.fact: Unity Hub is Unity's central launcher for managing projects, installs, and templates.
items.explanation: The Unity Hub allows developers to organize multiple Unity projects, install different versions of the Unity Editor, and access learning templates all from a single application.

items.title: Unity Learning Templates
items.fact: Unity offers learning templates that open fully guided, interactive experiences directly within the Unity Editor.
items.explanation: These templates provide structured, step-by-step tutorials that teach foundational skills like creating GameObjects, building simple gameplay, and incorporating audio and visual effects.

items.title: Unity Play Publishing
items.fact: Unity allows users to publish and share their games online through Unity Play.
items.explanation: After completing a project in Unity, developers can share their games with the community via Unity Play, allowing other learners to experience and provide feedback on their creations.

sources.title: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Experience Design
items.fact: Unity describes an experience-design stage that includes visual representations of the experience.
items.explanation: Designers can use sketches or more complex schematics to communicate how an experience should work.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: User Experience Flow
items.fact: The design stage can include mapping the user-experience flow or branching logic.
items.explanation: A flow map shows how users move through screens, choices, or interactions.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: UI Wireframe
items.fact: Unity lists creating UI wireframes as part of preliminary design work.
items.explanation: A wireframe represents the planned structure of an interface before detailed visual styling.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Concept Art
items.fact: Unity lists concept art and other visual design sketches as preliminary design work.
items.explanation: Concept art communicates visual direction before final assets are produced.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Prototype Evaluation
items.fact: Unity says prototypes are evaluated against defined user needs and game-design requirements.
items.explanation: A prototype is not only something to build; it is also something to test against the goals of the experience.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: External User Feedback
items.fact: Unity notes that prototype evaluation may seek feedback from target users.
items.explanation: Outside feedback can reveal problems or opportunities that the development team did not notice internally.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Iterative Design
items.fact: Unity describes iterative development as a cycle of design, build, test, evaluate, and refine.
items.explanation: Iteration means repeatedly improving the design using evidence from testing and evaluation.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Design Sign-Off
items.fact: Unity describes an iterative cycle beginning after prototypes are signed off by project decision-makers.
items.explanation: A sign-off marks a point at which the team agrees that a prototype is ready to move into a broader development cycle.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Regular Testing
items.fact: Unity says regular testing continues during iterative design and development.
items.explanation: Testing is part of the development cycle rather than only a final step before launch.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Internal Testing
items.fact: Unity notes that experiences usually undergo extensive internal testing before launch.
items.explanation: Team members can test the product repeatedly to find problems and verify intended behavior.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: External Testing
items.fact: Unity notes that experiences can also undergo external testing and user-feedback cycles before launch.
items.explanation: People outside the core development team can provide another source of usability and gameplay feedback.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Proof of Concept
items.fact: Unity describes chosen prototypes as proof of concept for full design and development.
items.explanation: A successful prototype can demonstrate that a design idea is workable before a larger production effort begins.

source.name: Unity Learn: Introduction to real-time 3D experience design

items.title: Asset Inventory
items.fact: Unity includes an asset inventory as an assignment in its prototyping project.
items.explanation: An asset inventory records the content a project expects to need, making production planning more concrete.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: Prototyping Practice
items.fact: Unity's course planning material includes creating prototypes with Unity as a learning goal.
items.explanation: A prototype lets designers and developers explore a game idea before committing to full production.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: Backlog
items.fact: Unity includes a backlog assignment in its milestones and agile-development project.
items.explanation: A backlog is a list of work items that can be prioritized and addressed during development.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: CRC Cards
items.fact: Unity includes Class-Responsibility-Collaboration cards as part of its milestone assignment.
items.explanation: CRC cards are a planning technique for thinking about classes, their responsibilities, and how they collaborate.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: Vertical Slice
items.fact: Unity includes building a vertical slice as a milestone assignment.
items.explanation: A vertical slice demonstrates the core of a game at a more complete level than a simple isolated prototype.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: Feature and Asset List
items.fact: Unity's vertical-slice planning step begins by identifying the core of the game and listing needed features and assets.
items.explanation: The list connects production work to the game's central experience.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: Peer Assessment
items.fact: Unity's project plan includes providing peer assessment on another learner's build.
items.explanation: Peer review adds outside evaluation to a development milestone.

source.name: Unity Learn: Course Introduction and Planning

items.title: Video Game History Foundation Digital Library
items.fact: The Video Game History Foundation Digital Library contains more than 30,000 curated files spanning 50 years of video game history.
items.explanation: The VGHF Digital Library is a free, publicly accessible archive for studying video game history. It includes out-of-print gaming magazines, rare press materials, trade publications, work documents, and exclusive interviews from both released and unreleased titles.

items.title: Founding of the Video Game History Foundation
items.fact: The Video Game History Foundation was founded on February 27, 2017, by Frank Cifaldi.
items.explanation: The foundation was established to catalog and digitize video game history materials that were at risk of being lost. Since its founding, it has built a massive archive that serves as an invaluable resource for game historians, developers, and enthusiasts.

items.title: Universal Scene Description (USD)
items.fact: Universal Scene Description (USD) is an open-source framework developed by Pixar for collaboratively constructing, editing, and reading complex 3D scenes.
items.explanation: USD allows multiple artists in different departments—such as lighting, animation, and modeling—to simultaneously work on the exact same 3D scene without overriding each other's files. It layers changes non-destructively, making large studio pipelines highly efficient.

items.title: Ptex Texture Mapping
items.fact: Ptex is a texture mapping system developed by Walt Disney Animation Studios that eliminates the need for UV assignment.
items.explanation: Traditional texturing requires artists to unwrap a 3D model into flat UV maps. Ptex avoids this tedious process by assigning a separate texture seamlessly to each face of a polygon mesh, streamlining the workflow for complex characters.

items.title: glTF
items.fact: glTF is a specification for runtime 3D asset delivery.
items.explanation: It is designed for transmitting and loading 3D scenes and models efficiently.

items.title: glTF Version
items.fact: The current glTF version listed by the Khronos registry is 2.0.
items.explanation: The registry identifies glTF 2.0 as the current specification line.

items.title: glTF Specification Updates
items.fact: Khronos notes that glTF 2.0 receives backwards-compatible clarifications and formatting improvements in patch updates.
items.explanation: Patch versions can refine the specification without changing its basic compatibility model.

items.title: glTF Extensions
items.fact: The Khronos registry maintains an extension registry for glTF 2.0.
items.explanation: Extensions expand the standard asset format while being documented separately.

items.title: OpenGL Graphics System Specification
items.fact: The OpenGL Registry contains specifications of the core API and shading language.
items.explanation: The OpenGL specification defines exactly how the API should work, ensuring consistent behavior across different hardware and operating systems. The Khronos Group maintains the official specification as the authoritative reference for developers.

items.title: OpenGL ES for Embedded Systems
items.fact: OpenGL ES is a royalty-free, cross-platform API for full-function 2D and 3D graphics on embedded systems.
items.explanation: OpenGL ES (Embedded Systems) provides a streamlined graphics API that balances performance with power efficiency on resource-constrained devices. It powers graphics on billions of mobile devices, gaming consoles, and vehicles worldwide.

items.title: OpenGL ES Versions
items.fact: The current version of OpenGL ES is OpenGL ES 3.2, with specifications for older versions also available.
items.explanation: OpenGL ES has evolved through versions 1.0, 1.1, 2.0, 3.0, 3.1, and 3.2. Each version added new features and capabilities, with version 3.2 being the most current standard for embedded graphics.

items.title: OpenXR Reference Space
items.fact: OpenXR defines reference spaces for spatial tracking.
items.explanation: A reference space provides a coordinate frame in which tracked positions and orientations are interpreted.

items.title: View Space
items.fact: OpenXR defines a VIEW reference space associated with the primary viewer's view origin.
items.explanation: It represents a viewer-centered spatial reference for supported XR rendering tasks.

items.title: Local Space
items.fact: OpenXR defines a LOCAL reference space type.
items.explanation: It provides a standard reference frame for local tracking scenarios.

items.title: Stage Space
items.fact: OpenXR defines a STAGE reference space type.
items.explanation: It is one of the standardized reference-space options in the specification.

items.title: Action
items.fact: OpenXR applications communicate input using actions.
items.explanation: An action represents an application-level interaction instead of a particular hardware control.

items.title: Action Set
items.fact: OpenXR groups actions into action sets.
items.explanation: An action set can organize related inputs for a usage context.

items.title: Interaction Profile
items.fact: OpenXR interaction profiles describe how actions can be bound to physical input devices.
items.explanation: Profiles connect application-level actions with controller-specific inputs.

items.title: Pose Action
items.fact: OpenXR supports pose actions.
items.explanation: A pose action can describe the location and orientation of a tracked input or object.

items.title: Haptic Event
items.fact: OpenXR supports haptic events through the action system.
items.explanation: Applications can use the XR interaction system to request tactile feedback.

items.title: Astro Boy's Original Manga Run
items.fact: According to Tezuka Productions' official site, the Astro Boy manga by Osamu Tezuka was serialized in a monthly boys' magazine from 1952 until 1968.
items.explanation: The manga predates the well-known 1963 television adaptation by more than a decade, showing how long the character existed in print before becoming a TV series.

items.title: Astro Boy as Japan's First 30-Minute Animated Series
items.fact: Tezuka Productions describes the 1963 Astro Boy television series as the first Japanese animated series to run in a 30-minute format, helping establish the foundation for later Japanese animation.
items.explanation: Establishing a standard episode length was part of what allowed Japanese TV animation to become a regular, ongoing industry rather than a series of one-off experiments.

items.title: Ptex Texture Mapping System
items.fact: Ptex is a texture mapping system developed by Walt Disney Animation Studios for production-quality rendering.
items.explanation: Ptex eliminates the need for UV assignment by storing texture data per-face on subdivision or polygon meshes. It became an important example of production graphics technology released as open source.

items.title: Picture Scrolls
items.fact: Web Japan identifies narrative picture scrolls drawn in the 12th century as part of the cultural history discussed in relation to anime.
items.explanation: These scrolls tell stories through sequences of pictures.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Choju Jinbutsu Giga
items.fact: Web Japan describes the first volume of Choju Jinbutsu Giga as a 12th-century picture scroll showing animals acting like people.
items.explanation: The work uses sequential drawn imagery for storytelling.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Exaggerated Imagery
items.fact: Web Japan notes the simple lines and exaggerated imagery of the Choju Jinbutsu Giga example.
items.explanation: Exaggerated forms can make characters and actions visually clear.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Ukiyo-e
items.fact: Web Japan identifies ukiyo-e woodblock prints as one of the artistic forms discussed in relation to manga and anime history.
items.explanation: Woodblock printing provided a means to reproduce illustrated imagery.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Commercial Manga Book
items.fact: Web Japan states that a 1720 Osaka book was the first manga book published for commercial purposes.
items.explanation: The item is part of the article's history of commercially reproduced illustrated storytelling.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Japanese Shadow Pictures
items.fact: Web Japan describes Japanese shadow pictures beginning in the 1750s as cut-paper storytelling images.
items.explanation: Cut paper and light were combined to create animated-looking visual narratives.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Edo Woodblock Mass Production
items.fact: Web Japan notes that during the Edo period artists developed woodblock techniques for mass production of illustrated books and prints.
items.explanation: Woodblock processes enabled illustrated content to be reproduced at scale.

source.name: NIPPONIA: Origins of Anime in Ancient Japanese Art

items.title: Anime Pop Culture
items.fact: Web Japan describes anime as Japanese animated pop culture with a worldwide audience.
items.explanation: The feature examines the evolution of Japanese animation into an industry and pop-culture phenomenon.

source.name: NIPPONIA: The Worldwide Phenomenon of Animé

items.title: Mobile Suit Gundam
items.fact: Web Japan describes Mobile Suit Gundam as a science-fiction anime centered on a conflict between space-based cities and the Earth Federation.
items.explanation: The series uses a large-scale political and technological setting for its story.

source.name: NIPPONIA: The Worldwide Phenomenon of Animé

items.title: Akira Influence
items.fact: Web Japan states that Katsuhiro Otomo's Akira was among cyberpunk anime that created a model that influenced films such as The Matrix.
items.explanation: The article connects Japanese animated science fiction with later live-action science fiction cinema.

source.name: NIPPONIA: The Worldwide Phenomenon of Animé

items.title: Ghost in the Shell Influence
items.fact: Web Japan states that Ghost in the Shell: Stand Alone Complex was among cyberpunk anime discussed as part of a model that influenced films such as The Matrix.
items.explanation: The article presents the series within a broader international influence discussion.

source.name: NIPPONIA: The Worldwide Phenomenon of Animé

items.title: Evangelion Influence
items.fact: Web Japan includes Neon Genesis Evangelion among cyberpunk anime discussed as influencing a model used by films such as The Matrix.
items.explanation: The source places the series within an international exchange of science-fiction visual ideas.

items.title: Manga-Anime Relationship
items.fact: Web Japan describes manga as an ancestor of anime and emphasizes their interdependent relationship.
items.explanation: Manga provides a major source of stories and characters for anime.

source.name: NIPPONIA: The Worldwide Phenomenon of Animé

items.title: 1970s Anime Exports
items.fact: Web Japan states that full-fledged exports of anime titles began in the 1970s.
items.explanation: The period marked an important phase in the international distribution of Japanese television animation.

items.title: Astro Boy Overseas
items.fact: Web Japan reports that Astro Boy gained popularity in Asia and the United States.
items.explanation: The series was an early example of Japanese animation traveling across borders.

items.title: Mazinger Z Europe
items.fact: Web Japan reports that Mazinger Z became a hit in Europe.
items.explanation: The series contributed to the international spread of Japanese animated television.

items.title: Pokemon Global Broadcast
items.fact: Web Japan reports that the Pokemon television series was eventually broadcast in more than 60 countries.
items.explanation: International television distribution helped the franchise reach a wide global audience.

items.title: Anime Themes
items.fact: Web Japan describes anime as covering themes including action heroes, space operas, martial arts, monster battles, school life, and fantasy.
items.explanation: The source shows that anime includes a broad range of genres and subjects.

items.title: Computerized Production
items.fact: Web Japan reports that coloring and animation processes that were once completely handmade were rapidly becoming computerized.
items.explanation: Digital tools changed parts of anime production workflows.

items.title: Academy Software Foundation Open Source
items.fact: The Academy Software Foundation hosts open source projects used throughout the motion picture industry.
items.explanation: Projects like OpenEXR, MaterialX, OpenVDB, OpenColorIO, and Open Shading Language are managed by the Academy Software Foundation. These tools standardize image processing and other critical workflows in film and VFX production.

items.title: Disney and the Academy Software Foundation
items.fact: Disney is a Founding Member of the Academy Software Foundation and an integral player in the open source community.
items.explanation: Disney has contributed to multiple projects including DPEL, MaterialX, OpenEXR, and OpenVDB. OpenColorIO is a key part of color management for Walt Disney Animation Studios.

items.title: OpenColorIO Color Management
items.fact: OpenColorIO is a color management solution used throughout the motion picture industry.
items.explanation: OpenColorIO provides a consistent color pipeline across different software and hardware. It is a key part of color management for studios like Walt Disney Animation Studios and is used in visual effects, animation, and post-production.

items.title: OpenEXR Image Format
items.fact: OpenEXR is a high dynamic-range (HDR) image file format developed for use in computer imaging applications.
items.explanation: OpenEXR is the professional-grade image storage format of the motion picture industry. It was originally developed by Industrial Light & Magic and has contributions from Walt Disney Animation Studios, Pixar, DreamWorks, and others.

items.title: Character Rigging in Maya
items.fact: Character rigging in Maya is the process of giving a 3D model a skeleton so it can move.
items.explanation: Maya provides tools like the Joint Tool to create bones and Inverse Kinematics (IK) and Forward Kinematics (FK) systems to control them. Facial rigging allows blend shapes and joint-based rigging for facial expressions.

items.title: Cel Animation
items.fact: Patented by Earl Hurd in 1914, cel animation involves drawing characters on transparent celluloid sheets laid over a stationary background.
items.explanation: Before this invention, animators had to redraw the background for every single frame of action. By using transparent layers, studios saved massive amounts of time, standardizing the animation workflow for the rest of the 20th century.

items.title: Winsor McCay and Cel Animation
items.fact: Winsor McCay's 1918 film The Sinking of the Lusitania was one of the first films to use cel animation, drawing scene elements on clear celluloid sheets rather than redrawing full backgrounds each time.
items.explanation: Cel animation became a foundational technique because it let animators reuse a static background while only redrawing the moving character on a separate transparent layer.

items.title: The Zoetrope
items.fact: Invented in 1834 by William George Horner, the zoetrope was an early optical device that created the illusion of motion from a sequence of static pictures.
items.explanation: The device consisted of a cylinder with vertical slits cut into its sides. When a user spun the cylinder and looked through the slits, the sequential drawings on the inside appeared to move due to the persistence of vision.

items.title: Astro Boy
items.fact: Astro Boy, created by Osamu Tezuka in 1963, was the first popular animated Japanese television series and established many stylistic foundations of anime.
items.explanation: Tezuka pioneered techniques such as reduced animation (using fewer frames per second to save time and budget) and large, expressive eyes. These stylistic and production choices became defining characteristics of the global anime industry.

items.title: Astro Boy and the Look of Anime
items.fact: Encyclopaedia Britannica identifies the 1963 broadcast of Astro Boy, created by Osamu Tezuka, as the first animation-only television series to establish the visual aesthetic associated with Japanese anime.
items.explanation: Before Astro Boy, Japanese animated works for television were less common, and the series is credited with helping spark a broader boom in Japanese TV animation.

items.title: Gertie the Dinosaur
items.fact: Winsor McCay's 1914 film Gertie the Dinosaur featured the first character ever created specifically for animated film, rather than adapted from a newspaper comic strip.
items.explanation: Most cartoon characters of that early era began as comic-strip figures first; Gertie was designed from the start as an animated performer.

items.title: The Scale of Hand-Drawn Animation
items.fact: Gertie the Dinosaur was composed of more than 10,000 individual drawings, with McCay redrawing the background by hand in nearly every frame.
items.explanation: At the time, no technique yet existed for keeping backgrounds and stationary objects consistent between frames, so the artist had to recreate them repeatedly.

items.title: Magnavox Odyssey
items.fact: Released in 1972 and designed by Ralph Baer, the Magnavox Odyssey was the first commercial home video game console.
items.explanation: It lacked sound and color graphics, relying on plastic overlays placed physically over the television screen to provide visual context for the games, but it successfully proved the concept of playing games on a home TV.

items.title: Pong
items.fact: Released by Atari in 1972, Pong was the first commercially successful video game and helped establish the video game industry.
items.explanation: Designed by Allan Alcorn, the game simulated table tennis using simple 2D graphics. Its massive success in arcades demonstrated that electronic games could be a highly profitable entertainment medium.

items.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
items.fact: Released in 1937 by Walt Disney, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs was the first full-length, traditionally animated feature film.
items.explanation: Critics initially called the project 'Disney's Folly', believing audiences would not sit through a feature-length cartoon. The film's unprecedented success proved that animated features could achieve deep emotional resonance and massive commercial viability.

items.title: Spacewar!
items.fact: Created in 1962 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Spacewar! is widely recognized as the first interactive computer game.
items.explanation: Developed by Steve Russell and other students on a PDP-1 computer, the game featured two player-controlled spaceships attempting to shoot each other while maneuvering around the gravitational pull of a central star.

items.title: Toy Story as the First Fully Computer-Animated Feature
items.fact: Toy Story, directed by John Lasseter and released in 1995, is recognized by Encyclopaedia Britannica as the first entirely computer-animated feature-length film.
items.explanation: Its production was a joint effort between Pixar Animation Studios and Walt Disney Pictures, marking a turning point for computer animation in mainstream filmmaking.

items.title: The Rendering Scale of Toy Story
items.fact: Pixar reported that producing Toy Story required 114,240 frames of computer animation and about 800,000 machine hours, rendering content at a maximum rate of 3.5 minutes of finished footage per week.
items.explanation: This figure illustrates how computationally demanding early full-length computer animation was compared to modern rendering hardware.

items.title: Brown Box

items.title: Computer Space
items.fact: Computer Space was released in 1971 as an early electronic arcade game.
items.explanation: The machine was based on the space-battle idea represented by Spacewar! and used no microprocessor, RAM, or ROM.

items.title: La Faim
items.fact: La Faim debuted in 1974 as a computer-assisted animation project involving Peter Foldes and Nestor Burtnyk.
items.explanation: The work used computer keyframe animation techniques to generate intermediate frames.

items.title: Computer Inbetweening

items.title: Road to Point Reyes
items.fact: The Road to Point Reyes is described by the Computer History Museum as an important early computer graphics image.

items.title: Early Rendering Cost
items.fact: The Computer History Museum records that a single Road to Point Reyes image took a month to render.
items.explanation: The example illustrates the large computational cost of early high-quality computer graphics.

items.title: Atari VCS

items.explanation: The console connected to a home television and used the MOS 6507 microprocessor.

items.title: Disney Animation Open Source Commitment
items.fact: Walt Disney Animation Studios is committed to advancing technology through sharing Open Source Software and Data Sets.
items.explanation: Disney Animation actively contributes to the open source community as a founding member of the Academy Software Foundation. Technologies developed at the studio, such as OpenEXR, OpenColorIO, and SeExpr, are available for public use.

items.title: Disney Animation Data Sets
items.fact: Walt Disney Animation Studios provides downloadable data sets from its animated films for research purposes.
items.explanation: These data sets are made available to inspire and enable research in computer graphics and animation. They provide valuable resources for academics, students, and developers studying animation technology.

items.title: Artist-Technologist Collaboration
items.fact: Disney Animation describes artists and technologists working together to advance animation.
items.explanation: Production technology is developed alongside artistic needs.

items.title: Open Source Technology
items.fact: Disney Animation publishes selected open-source software and datasets.
items.explanation: Some studio technology is shared with the wider technical community.

items.title: Film Datasets
items.fact: Disney Animation provides datasets from animated films for research.
items.explanation: The datasets allow technical users to study production-related information.

items.title: Technical Publications
items.fact: Disney Animation publishes technology work in academic journals and industry conferences.
items.explanation: Production technology can be communicated through formal technical publications.

items.title: Renderer
items.fact: A renderer takes models, animations, textures, lights, and other scene objects and produces a final image.
items.explanation: Rendering converts a scene description into the image seen by the viewer.

items.title: Light Transport
items.fact: Disney describes rendering as calculating how light bounces around a virtual scene.
items.explanation: Light transport determines how illumination reaches and interacts with surfaces.

items.title: Shading
items.fact: The renderer shades scene objects.
items.explanation: Shading determines their visible appearance under the scene's lighting conditions.

items.title: Hyperion
items.fact: Hyperion is Walt Disney Animation Studios' in-house renderer.
items.explanation: It is an internal rendering technology used by the studio.

items.title: Physically Based Path Tracer
items.fact: Disney describes Hyperion as a physically based path tracer.
items.explanation: Its rendering method follows light paths through the virtual scene.

items.title: Path Tracing
items.fact: Path tracing generates images by simulating how light interacts with objects in a virtual world.
items.explanation: Rays are traced through the scene and their surface interactions contribute to the final image.

items.title: Ray Bounces
items.fact: In path tracing, a ray can bounce between objects in the virtual scene.
items.explanation: Repeated light interactions contribute additional illumination.

items.title: Full Light Path
items.fact: Disney explains that path tracing calculates the path from a light source toward the camera.
items.explanation: The name comes from tracing the full route through which light contributes to an image.

items.title: glTF Format
items.fact: glTF is an open standard 3D file format developed by Khronos Group designed for the efficient transmission and loading of 3D scenes and models.
items.explanation: Often referred to as the JPEG of 3D, the glTF format minimizes the size of 3D assets and reduces the processing power needed to unpack and use them. This makes it highly efficient for rendering graphics on the web and in real-time applications.

items.title: glTF 1.0 Ratification
items.fact: The Khronos Group finalized and ratified the glTF 1.0 specification on October 19, 2015, describing it as an efficient, interoperable format for transmitting and loading 3D content.
items.explanation: glTF was created to solve a problem: unlike images or video, 3D content lacked a simple, widely shared data format before glTF's introduction.

items.title: OpenXR as a Cross-Platform Standard
items.fact: OpenXR is a royalty-free, open standard created by the Khronos Group that provides high-performance, cross-platform access to virtual reality and augmented reality devices, collectively called XR.
items.explanation: Before OpenXR, developers often had to write separate code for each headset's own API; OpenXR aims to let one application run across many XR platforms.

items.title: OpenXR 1.0 and Backward Compatibility
items.fact: When Khronos released the OpenXR 1.0 specification on July 29, 2019, the working group committed to maintaining full backward compatibility with the standard from that point onward.
items.explanation: This commitment gives hardware makers and software developers confidence that XR applications built for OpenXR will keep working as the standard evolves.

items.title: OpenXR 1.1 Consolidation
items.fact: Khronos released the OpenXR 1.1 specification on April 15, 2024, folding widely used API extensions into the core standard to reduce fragmentation across XR platforms.
items.explanation: Consolidating extensions into the core spec means developers can rely on more features being available by default, without needing to check for optional extensions.

items.title: OpenGL Shading Language (GLSL)
items.fact: The OpenGL Shading Language (GLSL) is the principal shading language for OpenGL.
items.explanation: GLSL allows developers to write shaders that run on the GPU, enabling advanced visual effects like Phong shading, bump mapping, and procedural textures. It is supported directly by OpenGL without extensions.

items.title: OpenXR
items.fact: OpenXR is a royalty-free standard that provides high-performance access to Virtual Reality (VR) and Augmented Reality (AR) platforms and devices.
items.explanation: Before OpenXR, developers had to write different code to support an Oculus headset versus an HTC Vive. OpenXR acts as a universal translator, allowing developers to write their code once and have it run seamlessly across a wide variety of XR headsets.

items.title: Vulkan API
items.fact: Vulkan is a low-overhead, cross-platform graphics API that provides high-efficiency access to modern graphics processing units (GPUs).
items.explanation: Unlike older graphics APIs, Vulkan gives developers direct control over how the GPU manages its memory and processes rendering tasks. This reduces CPU bottlenecks and allows games to draw vastly more detailed environments at higher framerates.

items.title: WebGL
items.fact: WebGL is a JavaScript API used to render interactive 2D and 3D graphics within any compatible web browser without the use of plug-ins.
items.explanation: WebGL brings the power of computer graphics hardware directly to the internet. It allows websites to display complex, fully interactive 3D models and games natively inside a standard web page.
